title: Physics models
text: The Tier A analytic models. At M0 they exercise the loop, the guard and the tests without any external code; they also serve as the fallbacks in toy runs. None of them is a physics claim about a real plasma. The one model meant for real scenarios, the Gaussian RF source, is at the end.

title: Physics models
text: The Tier A analytic models. At M0 they exercise the loop, the guard and the tests without any external code; they also serve as the fallbacks in toy runs. None of them is a physics claim about a real plasma. The one model meant for real scenarios, the Gaussian RF source, is at the end.

title: Physics models
text:
Circular equilibrium
Large-aspect-ratio circular flux surfaces with a prescribed parabolic safety factor, independent of the profiles. With \(r = a\rho\):
\[V = 2\pi^2 R_0 r^2,\quad V' = 4\pi^2 R_0 a^2 \rho,\quad G = \frac{1}{a^2},\quad
q = q_0 + (q_a - q_0)\rho^2,\]
\[\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\rho} = \frac{2\pi a^2 B_0\,\rho}{q}\ \ (\psi(0) = 0,\ \text{trapezoidal integration}),
\qquad I_p = \frac{2\pi a^2 B_0}{\mu_0 R_0 q_a}.\]
For this geometry, and only for it, the toroidal-flux radius at the boundary equals \(a\) (see K-007).

title: Physics models
text:
Critical-gradient transport
A smooth placeholder for stiff turbulent transport (OQ-1):
\[\chi = \chi_\min + \chi_\text{stiff}\, w\, \operatorname{softplus}\!\left(\frac{R/L_T - (R/L_T)_\text{crit}}{w}\right),
\qquad D_e = \frac{D}{\chi}\,\chi_e, \qquad v_e = v_\text{pinch}\,\rho .\]
Applied separately to \(\chi_e\) (from \(R/L_{T_e}\)) and \(\chi_i\) (from \(R/L_{T_i}\)). Softplus instead of a hard threshold, deliberately: the model has to be differentiable. The width \(w\) sets how stiff it is; the original M0 settings (\(\chi_\text{stiff} = 1\), \(w = 1\)) made relaxed Picard iteration oscillate, which is what motivated Newton (OQ-4). Its domain is unbounded, so it never asks for a fallback. Tested by tests/physics/test_monotonic.py (near the floor well below threshold, stiff well above it; more heating power gives higher temperatures).

title: Physics models
text:
Gaussian sources
Heating and particle sources with Gaussian radial shapes, normalised so the volume integral equals the configured total exactly on the discrete grid:
\[S(\rho_i) = S_\text{tot}\,\frac{\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 ((\rho_i - \rho_\text{dep})/w)^2\right)}{\sum_j \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12((\rho_j - \rho_\text{dep})/w)^2\right) V'_j\,\Delta\rho_j}.\]

title: Physics models
text:
Sawtooth placeholder
The identity. A smoothed-trigger model is part of the brief’s design; runs through TORAX use TORAX’s sawtooth model where the scenario enables one (neither ITER hybrid scenario does).

title: Physics models
text:
Gaussian RF heating
M1 asks for an analytic Gaussian radio-frequency deposition model. It will be the trusted fallback for an RF-deposition surrogate at M3, so it is a named model rather than a one-off config. TORAX already has one (its electron-cyclotron source: a Gaussian in \(\rho\) of chosen centre and width, normalised to the requested power, all to electrons, with optional co-located current drive), so the Tokamak Toolkit’s model is a typed wrapper over it, not a second implementation:
# tkit/physics/rf.py @ ae294c9 (trimmed)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GaussianRF:
    p_total: float                          #: absorbed power [W]
    rho_dep: float                          #: deposition centre in rho_tor_norm [-]
    width: float                            #: Gaussian width in rho_tor_norm [-]
    current_drive_efficiency: float = 0.0   #: TORAX ECCD efficiency, 0 = heating only [-]

    def torax_source(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {"P_total": self.p_total, "gaussian_location": self.rho_dep,
                "gaussian_width": self.width,
                "current_drive_efficiency": self.current_drive_efficiency}
Invalid inputs (negative power, centre outside \([0,1]\), non-positive width) are rejected at construction. Tests run the ITER hybrid scenario with 10 MW deposited at \(\rho = 0.4\):

title: Provenance and tracking
text:
The record
Beside every artifact <name> sits <name>.provenance.json. Reading an artifact through the toolkit reads and validates its record; a missing or malformed record is an error, not a warning.

The commit is read at import, not at write time (since 2 Oct 2026). A cluster job runs from the repository’s working copy, and commits can land there while it runs. Read at write time, git_sha named whatever the working copy’s HEAD had become: the third ASCOT5 job started at fcd8ce5 and its files record 2138b3c (entry 15). The process’s code is fixed when it is imported, so that is when the commit is read. The earlier ASCOT5 jobs may carry the same error; each job log prints the commit it started at.
Validation recomputes, not just inspects (since 2 Oct 2026, after a code review). Reading a record recomputes the config hash from the stored config, checks that every input digest is a sha256, and checks the artifact’s bytes against the recorded digest; an edited config or a replaced file is an error. A derived artifact’s tier is computed from its parents: B if any parent is B or of unknown tier, so gated data cannot pass on a Tier A label. Because each parent is recorded by content hash with its path and tier, an artifact copied elsewhere still names what it was made from. Records written before schema 2 are still read, under the hash convention they were written with, but they carry no artifact digest; a consumer that needs the binding (handing ASCOT5 heating back to TORAX) refuses them unless told explicitly, and then records the lineage as acknowledged, not verified. Tested by tests/unit/test_tracking.py and tests/unit/test_provenance_integrity.py.
Examples in use: TORAX reference runs (scenario, TORAX version, the full resolved TORAX config); the MAST-U machine description (upstream URL at the pinned commit, licence, sha256 of each file, checked against pinned digests before the files are loaded); saved FreeGSNKE equilibria (machine, FreeGSNKE version, upstream commit, the solve settings and coil currents, and the machine files by hash); ASCOT5 alpha heating profiles (the TORAX state’s time, and the TORAX run, ASCOT5 file and EQDSK they came from, by hash, with the ASCOT5 build).

title: Provenance and tracking
text:
Run tracking
Purpose. A record of every run that a person can browse, compare and be alerted from, without the simulation ever depending on it. It serves invariant 4 (nothing impure inside compiled code) and §9 of the brief (stalls are reported, not hidden).
What is recorded. Every command that runs physics (the toy scenario, a TORAX whole-code run, The Tokamak Toolkit’s fixed-step loop over TORAX, a free-boundary equilibrium) opens a run. A local record is always written, as a directory per run:







file
content




provenance.json, config.yaml
the provenance record above, and the resolved configuration


params.json
run parameters (scenario, time step, step count, tolerance, device, code versions)


metrics.jsonl
one line per simulation step, with the step number, the simulation time, and the series below; then headline numbers (wall time, stored energy, fallback fraction, benchmark errors)


events.jsonl
free-text events, alerts, artifacts logged, and the final status


artifacts
copies of files written by the run, each with its provenance record



Per-step series: on-axis electron and ion temperature and density, stored thermal energy, the solver’s convergence state and iteration count, sawtooth crashes, the guard’s verdict and the fraction of radial faces handed to the fallback model (toy loop: also the final iteration residual and the ensemble spread of the transport coefficients).
Algorithm. The compiled loop returns its whole trace (one row per step) at the end. Only then, on the host, is each step’s row written as one metrics record. Nothing inside the compiled code calls the tracker, so tracking cannot change the numbers or the compiled program.
Alerts. A condition the owner must see raises a named alert, recorded in the event log, printed to the terminal, and sent to the mirror as a critical alert:







alert
raised when




picard_stall
a fixed-point step ends above its stall tolerance


solver_stall
TORAX’s nonlinear solver reports non-convergence on any step


benchmark_fail
a profile differs from its reference by more than the tolerance


torax_incomplete
a TORAX run ends without completing


non_finite_metric
a logged number is NaN or infinite (kept locally; the mirror rejects it)



A run is a context manager: if the simulation raises, the exception is logged as an event, the run ends with status failed, and the exception still propagates. A failed benchmark also ends the run failed: a profile or trace outside the agreed tolerance, a non-finite value, an incomplete simulation, or a failed balance check gives a nonzero exit and a failed run, and a comparison with no common output at the requested end time is an error, not a zero. Run directories are unique even for same-name runs started in the same second.
Mirrors. The local record can be mirrored to Simvue (Apache-2.0), a run-tracking server with a web dashboard, metric plots and alert notifications, or to MLflow. The mirror gets the same parameters, per-step metrics against simulation time, events, alerts, configuration, provenance (flattened into searchable metadata) and artifacts. Runs are filed by command and tagged with the tier, and the mirror’s run name matches the local directory, so the two can always be matched.
Compute nodes on the cluster have no internet access. Inside a batch job the mirror therefore runs in offline mode, caching everything locally; a script run later from a login node uploads the cache, and a run uploaded in several goes still lands as one run on the server.
Design decisions.

Local first, mirror second. The local record is always complete. If the mirror cannot start (no network, expired credentials), the run continues with a warning; a failure later in the run is reported once and ignored. Tracking must never cost a simulation.
Credentials never reach a log. The server’s own configuration errors echo the access token, so only the error message itself is ever printed.
Close, then mark failed. The mirror’s client discards its queue of unsent metrics if a run is marked failed while still open, so a failed run is first closed (flushing everything) and then given its failed status.

Correctness. tests/unit/test_tracking.py (local record, events, alerts, failed status on an exception, one record per step), tests/unit/test_simvue_tracking.py (the mirror receives what the local record holds; offline mode inside a batch job; a mirror that cannot start leaves the local record intact; the real client writing an offline cache with no network), and tests/regression/test_cli_tracking.py (the toy scenario end to end: 100 of 100 stepsC-040).

title: Invariants and environment
text: The rules every other section relies on, and for each one the mechanism that enforces it. A rule that exists only as a convention is marked as such.

title: Invariants and environment
text: The rules every other section relies on, and for each one the mechanism that enforces it. A rule that exists only as a convention is marked as such.

title: Invariants and environment
text:
Numerical and physical conventions
Float64 everywhere. Importing the package switches JAX to double precision (jax_enable_x64), because stiff transport and Newton iterations lose too much in single precision. Nothing turns it off.
# tkit/__init__.py @ 426e6ad
import jax

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
Units are strict SI except temperature in eV and density in m⁻³, matching IMAS (the full table is in the notation). Every array field of every state object carries its unit in a same-line docstring. Adapters are the only place unit conversion happens: inside the core, physics and surrogate packages there are no conversion factors apart from the elementary charge, used to turn eV into joules. Enforced by convention and review, not by a test.
One radial coordinate. Internally everything is on \(\rho\) (rho_tor_norm). Profiles and sources on cell centres, transport coefficients on faces. Conversions from other coordinates happen only in adapters. Convention.
No magic numbers. Every physical or numerical parameter is a typed config field with a unit docstring, serialised to YAML. Unknown keys are rejected, and scalars are coerced to their annotated type. That second rule exists because PyYAML implements YAML 1.1, under which 2.0e6 (an exponent without a sign) is a string, which would otherwise travel silently into a JAX array. Enforced by tests/unit/test_config.py.
Explicit randomness. Random keys are threaded through call signatures; there are no global seeds. Convention (nothing random runs in the simulation yet).

title: Invariants and environment
text:
Purity inside compiled code
The whole simulation compiles to one program. Inside it: no file I/O, no tracking or logging calls, and no Python if on a traced value. Tracking happens on the host after simulate returns. Loops are lax.scan of fixed length, never while_loop, so reverse-mode differentiation works and cost is predictable. Partly enforced: the differentiability tests (see tests) fail if an unbounded loop appears in a differentiated path. The purity rule is enforced by review only. An impure call inside jit does not fail: it runs once, silently, while the function is being traced, and never again, which is exactly why the rule exists.

title: Invariants and environment
text:
Building the external codes
Recorded because two of these took several attempts and the failure modes are not obvious.
Aurora 3.0.6. Its source distribution declares cmake.minimum-version and ninja.minimum-version, which scikit-build-core 0.8 and later reject. Replacing them with cmake.version = ">=3.17.2" and ninja.version = ">=1.10" in pyproject.toml fixes the build (with a Fortran compiler set via FC, and --no-build-isolation). The install silently downgrades NumPy to 1.26 and xarray to 2022.9, which breaks TORAX and JAX. Both are restored afterwards, Aurora’s Fortran core was checked to work under NumPy 2.4.6 despite its numpy<2 pin, and every later install uses a constraints file pinning NumPy and xarray. Atomic data (OPEN-ADAS) is not downloaded yet.
ASCOT5 (non-MPI). Built from source with three workarounds for the cluster’s toolchain:

the HDF5 compiler wrapper rejects a flag the build passes (-shlib), so the build uses plain gcc with explicit HDF5 include, library and rpath flags;
the system gcc is configured to offload OpenMP to GPUs, which breaks the final link, so the build passes -foffload=disable;
loading the compiler through the module system silently blocks the Python and CMake modules, so the compiler is used by its full path instead.

Then the Python bindings are installed without dependencies, under the NumPy/xarray constraints. A smoke test builds an analytic ITER magnetic field and checks its 1/R fall-off to 2%C-031.
FreeGSNKE 3.1.1 and the IMAS-Python pin. FreeGSNKE 3.1.1 declares imas-python>=2.3,<3; TORAX 1.4.3 pins imas-python==2.1.0. No resolver can satisfy both. FreeGSNKE uses only IDSFactory and DBEntry, both present in 2.1.0, so it is installed with --no-deps (and freegs4e separately), and its IMAS writer is exercised by the MAST-U tests. The CI workflow does not install the equilibrium extra for this reason, so those tests skip there.
Process CPU limit. The cluster’s interactive nodes kill any process after 600 s of CPU time, summed over threads. XLA’s multithreaded CPU backend reaches that quickly, so the suite is run as one process per test file.

title: TGLF datasets for MAST-U and ITER, version 1
text:
new component Entry 17 · milestone M2
The surrogates of M3 learn TGLF’s fluxes from examples (entry 16). The owner set one dataset per machine, MAST-U and ITER, so that either can be used alone or both pooled. Each dataset is a set of TGLF input points and the fluxes TGLF returns for them.

title: TGLF datasets for MAST-U and ITER, version 1
text:
How the points were chosen
Each TGLF input is a local description of the plasma at one radius. We split the inputs into two groups. The geometry inputs (major radius, elongation, triangularity and their radial derivatives, q, magnetic shear) were measured, not guessed: we computed them the way TORAX computes them, on the flux surfaces of real equilibria, and took each range from the 1st to 99th percentile. For MAST-U the equilibria are 42 FreeGSNKE free-boundary solutions on the MAST-U machine description. For ITER they are TORAX’s ITER hybrid equilibrium plus the q profiles of TORAX’s current ramp-up example. The kinetic inputs (temperature and density gradients, temperature ratio, beta, collisionality, effective charge, flow shear) were proposed by the agent and approved by the owner per machine (OQ-16). The generator refuses to write a dataset for a region until its kinetic inputs are marked approved.
The inputs are drawn by Latin hypercube sampling. Drawn independently, high beta and steep gradients combine into pressure gradients far beyond ballooning stability, where TGLF returned fluxes of 104 to 105 gyro-Bohm units in the timing run. Points are therefore rejected above a fixed normalised pressure gradient αMHD, set per machine for version 1; a cap that depends on the magnetic shear is to follow (OQ-16). The cap keeps about half the draws and shifts the kept set towards low q and low beta.

title: Datasets
text:
TGLF
TGLF is a quasilinear model of drift-wave turbulence from General Atomics’ GACODE suite, github.com/gafusion/gacode, Apache-2.0 (Tier A). For each point it solves a gyro-fluid eigenvalue problem over a grid of binormal wavenumbers and maps the linear growth rates to fluxes through a saturation rule. We use GACODE commit f34a9dd, built for the cluster’s CPU nodes (Zen 4), and call TGLF in-process through tglf2py, the wrapper TORAX uses, so the datasets and any later TGLF run inside TORAX use the same binary. CGYRO, the nonlinear gyrokinetic code from the same suite, is built from the same commit for spot checks of TGLF at M4 (OQ-15 c).
Install checks (TGLF 9/9 regression cases; tglf2py wrapper 11/11; TORAX TGLF transport-model tests 3/3; CGYRO 21/21C-069). TGLF’s regression cases run through the standalone binary and through the wrapper; TORAX’s TGLF transport-model tests; CGYRO’s regression suite. TORAX 1.4.3 needs one upstream TGLF fix, applied as a patch to the installed package and reapplied whenever the environment is rebuilt.

title: Datasets
text:
Sampling space

Inputs
A point is TGLF’s local input set at one radius, in TGLF’s names and TORAX’s conventions: lengths normalised to the minor radius \(a\) of the last closed flux surface, species 1 = electrons, 2 = main ion, 3 = impurity, masses relative to the deuteron. The inputs fall into three groups.
Geometry, measured. RMAJ_LOC, DRMAJDX_LOC, KAPPA_LOC, S_KAPPA_LOC, DELTA_LOC, S_DELTA_LOC, Q_LOC, SHAT. These are computed exactly as TORAX computes them from its geometry object when it builds TGLF inputs (checked against TORAX’s own input builder), on every flux-surface face with \(0.1 \le r/a \le 0.9\), for a set of equilibria per machine:

MAST-U: a 60-point Latin hypercube over FreeGSNKE’s MAST-U-like machine (plasma current, pressure scaling, vacuum field, profile exponents and three coil-current multipliers); 42 equilibria accepted (10 did not converge, 5 rejected, 3 timed out). LCFS elongation 1.71–2.28, aspect ratio 1.53–1.77, q95 3.8–9.8. Triangularity and its shear are taken from \(r/a \ge 0.6\) only: inside that, FreeGSNKE’s triangularity on its default grid is grid noise (K-013).
ITER: TORAX’s ITER hybrid equilibrium (EQDSK) at flat top, plus the q profiles of TORAX’s current ramp-up example (plasma current 3 to 10.5 MA, 41 output times) on the same shape. One shape only (K-016).

Each sampling range is the measured 1st–99th percentile, widened by 5% of its span on each side, rounded outward to 0.01, with triangularity and its shear floored at 0, elongation at 1 and q at 0.7. A unit test re-derives the ranges from the stored envelope, so the configuration cannot drift from the measurement.
Kinetic, approved. Proposed by the agent, approved per machine by the owner (OQ-16 a). The generator refuses to write a dataset for a region whose kinetic block is not marked approved.

The radius RMIN_LOC (\(r/a\)) is sampled uniformly over 0.1–0.9.
Derived, never sampled. From quasi-neutrality with a main ion of charge 1 and one impurity of charge \(Z\): \(n_3/n_e = (Z_\mathrm{eff}-1)/(Z(Z-1))\), \(n_2/n_e = 1 - Z\,n_3/n_e\). Ion and impurity gradients equal the main-ion ones, and \(T_3 = T_2\) (TORAX does not evolve the impurity temperature either). Then
\[
\texttt{Q\_PRIME\_LOC} = \frac{q^2}{(r/a)^2}\,\hat s, \qquad
\texttt{P\_PRIME\_LOC} = -\frac{q}{r/a}\,\frac{\beta_e}{8\pi}\sum_s \frac{n_s}{n_e}\frac{T_s}{T_e}
\left(\frac{a}{L_{n_s}} + \frac{a}{L_{T_s}}\right),
\]
\[
\alpha_\mathrm{MHD} = q^2\,\frac{R}{a}\,\beta_e \sum_s \frac{n_s}{n_e}\frac{T_s}{T_e}
\left(\frac{a}{L_{n_s}} + \frac{a}{L_{T_s}}\right) = -q^2 R\,\frac{d\beta}{dr},
\]
with \(\beta\) on Bunit. The P_PRIME_LOC expression is TORAX’s \(10^{-7}\,(dp/dr)\,q a^2/(r B_\mathrm{unit}^2)\) written in TGLF’s dimensionless inputs, checked against TORAX in a physics test.


The αMHD cap
Drawn independently, high \(\beta_e\) and steep gradients combine into pressure gradients far beyond ballooning stability. In the timing run, four MAST-U points of this kind returned 104–105 gyro-Bohm units. Over the uncapped box, αMHD has median 4.1 (MAST-U) and 2.9 (ITER), and 99th percentile 49 and 81. Version 1 rejects points above a fixed cap per machine (OQ-16 c). The cap does not depend on the magnetic shear, although an \(s\)–\(\alpha\) ballooning boundary does (K-017). Because αMHD grows as \(q^2\), the cap also removes most high-q points on ITER (MAST-U 0.490 kept (220936 drawn), ITER 0.425 (258597 drawn); kept mean beta_e 23-25% below the box mean on both; kept median q 1.90 (MAST-U) and 1.73 (ITER, sampled log-uniform over 1.02-11.1)C-073).


Algorithm 1: sampling a region (as in tkit.datasets.tglf_dataset.sample_region)
input: region ranges R (geometry + kinetic), log-uniform set L, cap A, seed s, target n
kept = [], drawn = 0, k = 0
while |kept| < n:
    acc = |kept| / drawn  (1 if drawn = 0)
    m   = max(64, ceil(1.2 (n - |kept|) / max(acc, 1e-3)))
    U   = LatinHypercube(dim = 1 + |R|, seed = 1000 s + k).random(m)
    for u in U:
        x = map u to [0.1, 0.9] for r/a and to R (log scale for inputs in L)
        if alpha_MHD(x) <= A: kept.append(x)
    drawn += m, k += 1
return kept[:n], acceptance = |kept| / drawn
Each batch is a separate Latin hypercube, so the union is stratified within batches but not across them. The result is reproducible from the seed (MAST-U 0, ITER 1).

title: Datasets
text:
Generation and storage

Sample the region (Algorithm 1) and save the points.
Run TGLF on the points in chunks of 4096, one process per core, each case with OMP_NUM_THREADS = 1. A case records the six fluxes, a status (0 finite, 1 non-finite, 2 TGLF error) and its wall time. A chunk file appears only once complete, so a job cut by its time limit resumes at the next chunk when resubmitted.
When all chunks exist, write tglf-<region>-v<k>.npz: inputs (sampled and derived, by name), outputs, status, wall times and the metadata (spec, sampling space version, region block, GACODE commit, TGLF settings, species, sampling statistics). Write the provenance record beside it: git commit and dirty flag, package versions, configuration hash, and the SHA-256 of the dataset file, the sampling-space file and the geometry record. Make the file read-only. A finished dataset is never rewritten; a change makes version \(k+1\).
Log per-chunk metrics (completed fraction, cases per second, mean wall time) and the final file with its provenance to the run tracker (Simvue). Inside a cluster job the tracker writes offline; the cache is uploaded from a login node, and the upload is checked by comparing the server’s checksum with the local SHA-256.

Outputs: \(\Gamma_e, \Gamma_i, \Gamma_\mathrm{imp}\) (particle fluxes) and \(Q_e, Q_i,
Q_\mathrm{imp}\) (heat fluxes), in TGLF’s gyro-Bohm units with UNITS = CGYRO. Loading a dataset recomputes the file’s SHA-256 and refuses it if it differs from the provenance record.

Design decisions

Geometry measured, not chosen (OQ-15 a). The agent’s first proposal, written from memory, had MAST-U triangularity up to 0.6 (an LCFS value); measured on interior surfaces it is at most 0.24.
One dataset per machine, not one pooled space (owner, 2026-10-02). Pooling is a training choice, made at M3 from the tags.

title: Learning without Convergence
text:
Consider a family of expectations indexed by a configuration \(a\):
\[
F(a)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim p(\cdot\mid a)}[f(a,\xi)].
\]
For one configuration, the usual Monte Carlo (MC) estimator is
\[
\hat F_N(a)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(a,\xi_i),
\qquad \xi_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim p(\cdot\mid a).
\]
With finite variance, the estimator’s root-mean-squared error decreases as \(N^{-1/2}\). Resolving each expectation independently can therefore be expensive.
To learn a surrogate \(G_\theta(a)\) across material properties, source distributions, or model parameters, a fixed budget can buy accurate labels at a few configurations or noisy labels at many.
Must each Monte Carlo estimate converge before it becomes useful training data?
For squared-error regression, conditionally unbiased labels preserve the clean population optimum, even when individual estimates are poor. Learning can pool evidence across configurations when their expectation map has shared structure.
Motivated by noisy particle-transport supervision in PTNO (Cao et al. 2026), we examine this equivalence, simulation allocation, and nonlinear target bias.

title: Learning without Convergence
text:
Learning from an unconverged estimator
Write the stochastic label as
\[
\hat F_N(a)=F(a)+\epsilon_N(a),
\qquad \mathbb E[\epsilon_N\mid a]=0.
\]
For a fixed configuration distribution \(\rho\), assume finite second moments and that the model receives \(a\) without access to its label’s random draws. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_N(\theta)
&=\mathbb E_{a,\xi}\big[(G_\theta(a)-\hat F_N(a))^2\big],\\
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{clean}}(\theta)
&=\mathbb E_a\big[(G_\theta(a)-F(a))^2\big].
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding the square, the cross term vanishes because \(\mathbb E[\epsilon_N\mid a]=0\), giving
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_N(\theta)
&=\mathcal L_{\mathrm{clean}}(\theta)\\
&\quad+\mathbb E[\epsilon_N^2].
\end{aligned}
\]
The noise term is independent of \(\theta\). Thus, over the same model class and whenever minimizers exist,
\[
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
\arg\min_\theta\mathcal L_N(\theta)\\
=\arg\min_\theta\mathcal L_{\mathrm{clean}}(\theta).
\end{gathered}}
\]
The identity holds for restricted model classes and squared vector or field norms. It preserves the best approximation within the class, rather than guaranteeing exact recovery of \(F\).
Finite-data accuracy, optimization, and extrapolation remain separate questions. High-variance labels can destabilize gradients or be memorized by a flexible model.
Noise2Noise established this principle in image restoration, including MC rendering (Lehtinen et al. 2018). Here, the input is a configuration. In both settings, unbiasedness must hold conditional on the model’s input; unconditional zero-mean noise is insufficient.

title: Learning without Convergence
section: Where should the simulation budget go?
text:
Where should the simulation budget go?
For \(M\) distinct configurations, \(N\) samples per label, and \(K\) independent labels per configuration, an equal-cost sample budget is
\[
\boxed{B=MKN.}
\]
If one sample has conditional variance \(\sigma^2(a)\), averaging the \(K\) labels gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left[
\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat F_N^{(k)}(a)\,\middle|\,a
\right]=\frac{\sigma^2(a)}{NK}.
\]
Thus \(N\) and \(K\) improve precision at known locations; \(M\) increases coverage. At fixed predictions, summing squared losses against \(K\) labels is equivalent to fitting their average, up to a constant and factor \(K\). Stochastic optimization can still depend on their presentation.
This is the established replication versus exploration problem: stochastic kriging separates simulator noise from response-surface uncertainty (Ankenman, Nelson, and Staum 2010), while sequential design chooses between repeated and new configurations (Binois et al. 2019).
For the Gaussian problem, we compare three allocations with \(B=4,096\), \(K=1\), identical training settings, and seeds 0–7. Within each seed, initialization and random-number streams are shared across allocations, with draws regrouped into configurations. Stored-label reuse adds training cost but no simulation draws.

PTNO finds benefits from broader coverage until saturation (Cao et al. 2026); CTMC moment-map learning finds different allocation needs for means and transformed covariances (Pratt and Prosper-Feldman 2026). Neither implies that \(N=1\) is universally optimal.
Unbiasedness locates the population optimum; efficient allocation depends on coverage, noise, model capacity, optimization, and simulation costs.

title: Learning without Convergence
section: Unbiasedness is fragile under nonlinear transformations
text:
Unbiasedness is fragile under nonlinear transformations
For a desired output \(g(F(a))\), squared-loss regression against transformed labels targets
\[
\mathbb E[g(\hat F_N(a))\mid a],
\]
which generally differs from \(g(F(a))\). More configurations do not remove this gap.
For positive estimates with an integrable logarithm, Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[\log\hat F_N(a)\mid a]
\leq \log F(a).
\]
At \(a=0\) and \(N=1\) in the Gaussian example, \(\hat F_1=Z^2\) with \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\mathbb E[\hat F_1]&=0,\\
\mathbb E[\log\hat F_1]
&=-\gamma-\log 2\approx-1.27036,
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\gamma\) is the Euler–Mascheroni constant.1 With 200,000 independent diagnostic draws, the log sample mean is \(0.00003\), while the mean natural log is \(-1.27193\) (SE \(0.00497\)). These draws are separate from training.
PTNO retains physical-space targets to avoid this bias; its prediction-normalized, stop-gradient loss requires a separate gradient analysis (Cao et al. 2026). Nonlinear Noise2Noise examines nonlinear maps and losses in MC denoising (Tinits and Mann 2025). A positive output parameterization can still be trained against unbiased, untransformed labels.
Clipping zero or negative estimates before taking logs changes the target again.

title: Learning without Convergence
text:
Learn primitive expectations first
Primitives are the component expectations of a derived quantity. Learn them from unbiased labels, then apply the desired formula to their predictions:
\[
\boxed{\begin{gathered}
\text{Learn primitives}\\
\text{from unbiased labels;}\\
\text{compose afterwards.}
\end{gathered}}
\]
For variance, these are the first two raw moments:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m_1(a)&=\mathbb E[X\mid a],\\
m_2(a)&=\mathbb E[X^2\mid a],\\
V(a)&=m_2(a)-m_1(a)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(N\) independent draws, \(\hat m_1=N^{-1}\sum_i X_i\) and \(\hat m_2=N^{-1}\sum_i X_i^2\) are unbiased. Squaring the noisy mean introduces bias. Writing \(m_1=m_1(a)\) and \(V=V(a)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[\hat m_1^2\mid a]
&=m_1^2+\frac{V}{N},\\
\mathbb E[\hat m_2-\hat m_1^2\mid a]
&=\left(1-\frac1N\right)V.
\end{aligned}
\]
With one sample, the plug-in variance label is always zero, even when the true variance is positive:
\[
\hat m_2-\hat m_1^2=X^2-X^2=0.
\]
Squared-loss training therefore targets zero, regardless of how many observations we collect.
Instead, train on \(X\) and \(X^2\) as separate labels, using \(a\) as input. Pool observations to learn their conditional means, then form
\[
V_\theta(a)=G_2(a)-G_1(a)^2.
\]
For the Gaussian example, the exact targets \(G_1(a)=a\) and \(G_2(a)=a^2+1\) give variance \(1\). One-sample supervision preserves these population targets.
Unbiased direct labels remain valid: for \(N>1\), Bessel-corrected sample variance can be learned directly. CTMC moment-map bias arises from preprocessing and Cholesky factorization of an unbiased sample covariance (Pratt and Prosper-Feldman 2026).
For a ratio \(R=A/D\), unbiased component estimates generally yield a biased ratio label. Learn \(A\) and \(D\) separately, then evaluate \(R_\theta=G_A/G_D\). If \(G_A=A+e_A\) and \(G_D=D+e_D\),
\[
R_\theta-\frac{A}{D}
=\frac{D e_A-A e_D}{D(D+e_D)}.
\]
Small denominators amplify errors; approximate moments can produce negative variances or lose precision through cancellation. Avoiding label bias does not guarantee an accurate composed prediction.

title: Learning without Convergence
text:
Where the simple theory breaks
Conditional unbiasedness fails or needs additional analysis in four common settings:

Finite-run MCMC. Initialization away from stationarity generally biases averages. Stationary initialization removes this bias; correlations still affect variance. Coupled methods can construct unbiased alternatives (Jacob, O’Leary, and Atchadé 2020).
Self-normalized estimators. Random normalization generally introduces finite-sample bias, as in the ratio example.
Nested MC. In \(\mathbb E_X[g(\mathbb E[Y\mid X])]\), a finite inner average followed by nonlinear \(g\) generally introduces bias. Increasing only outer samples can converge to the wrong target (Rainforth et al. 2018).
Biased simulators. Discretization, trajectory truncation, or approximate physics can shift the simulated mean away from the intended target, as PTNO notes (Cao et al. 2026).

With systematic bias,
\[
\hat F_N(a)=F(a)+b_N(a)+\epsilon_N(a),
\qquad \mathbb E[\epsilon_N\mid a]=0.
\]
Squared-loss learning targets \(F+b_N\), or its best approximation in the model class. More coverage cannot separate \(F\) from \(b_N\) without additional information. Recovering \(F\) requires higher fidelity, debiasing, or a model of the bias.

title: Learning without Convergence
section: How this connects to existing work
text:
How this connects to existing work
Learned MC methods improve estimators used at inference. Amortized MC Integration learns function-aware proposals; Target-Aware Bayesian Inference uses the integrand to guide sampling (Goliński, Wood, and Rainforth 2019; Rainforth et al. 2020). Neural Control Variates learns an integrable approximation and samples a residual correction (Müller et al. 2020). These retain stochastic inference, with guarantees determined by their correction and normalization schemes.
Expectation-map learning produces approximate deterministic predictions. Recent examples include WoS-NO’s stochastic PDE supervision, CTMC moment maps, and PTNO (Viswanath et al. 2026; Pratt and Prosper-Feldman 2026; Cao et al. 2026). WoS-NO also reports bias from early termination and caching, illustrating the gap between an ideal stochastic representation and its implementation.
Noisy regression and replication versus exploration are established foundations. The open question is when shared structure makes learning the expectation itself computationally efficient.

title: Learning without Convergence
text:
A broader hypothesis
The hypothesis is that convergence can be shared across configurations when their expectation map has learnable structure. Establishing when this is beneficial requires an allocation theory that accounts for coverage, estimator noise and bias, approximation, optimization, and training cost. When should stochastic computation converge locally, and when can its convergence be shared across related problems?

title: Learning without Convergence
section: Two deliberately noisy Monte Carlo examples
text:
Two deliberately noisy Monte Carlo examples
Consider
\[
X\mid a\sim\mathcal N(a,1),\qquad
F(a)=\mathbb E[X^2\mid a]=a^2+1.
\]
The sample mean of \(X^2\) is unbiased, even with \(N=1\):
\[
\hat F_1(a)=X^2,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[\hat F_N(a)\mid a]=\frac{2+4a^2}{N}.
\]
At \(a=3\), a single label has standard deviation \(\sqrt{38}\) around a mean of \(10\): substantial, configuration-dependent noise.
We train a \(1\to32\to32\to1\) MLP with tanh hidden layers and a linear output on one sample at each of 4,096 configurations drawn uniformly from \([-3,3]\). Training uses full-batch Adam, learning rate \(0.01\), 800 CPU updates, and fixed linear rescaling. Exact targets enter only evaluation and plotting, with no clean-label tuning or stopping.






Figure 1: All 4,096 one-sample labels and the learned expectation. The seed-0 model has 3.63% relative \(L_2\) error on the evaluation grid.



The shared model pools noisy observations to learn a simple conditional-mean map.

From individual trajectories to transport expectations
For a discrete transport example, start a symmetric random walk at \(x\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\}\) and stop at boundary \(0\) or \(L\). The exit time \(\tau\) and right-exit indicator \(H=\mathbf 1\{X_\tau=L\}\) satisfy (Aldous and Fill 2002, sec. 5.1)
\[
\mathbb E[H\mid x]=\frac{x}{L},
\qquad
\mathbb E[\tau\mid x]=x(L-x).
\]
One complete trajectory supplies two unbiased labels without evaluating either expectation:
def walk_label(x, rng, length=32):
    steps = 0
    while 0 < x < length:
        x += rng.choice([-1, 1])
        steps += 1
    return int(x == length), steps
With \(L=32\), we generate 4,096 independent trajectories from uniformly sampled starting sites among the 31 interior positions. Sites recur. A \(1\to32\to32\to2\) MLP learns both expectations with the same hidden layers and optimizer settings, dividing the input by \(L\) and duration labels by \(L^2\). Exact formulas are evaluation references.






Figure 2: Site-wise mean labels and learned expectations. Seed-0 relative \(L_2\) errors are 1.32% for escape probability and 3.91% for mean exit time.



Across seeds 0–7, these errors are \(1.66\pm0.45\%\) and \(3.87\pm1.07\%\) (mean ± sample SD). This illustrates pooling across a finite set of sites, without establishing an efficiency advantage. No trajectory is truncated; seed 0 uses 716,131 transitions, showing why trajectory counts alone obscure simulation cost.

title: Heat-flux positivity and monotonicity of TGLF in the gradients
text:
new component measurement Entry 20 · milestone M3
The brief asks for physics structure in the transport surrogates: zero heat flux below the instability threshold, no negative heat flux, and a heat flux that does not fall when its own temperature gradient rises. Without that structure a surrogate can return fluxes the transport solver treats as unphysical. The owner decided in OQ-19 to put a ReLU on the electron and ion heat fluxes, \(Q_e\) and \(Q_i\), and to measure monotonicity on TGLF before imposing it.

title: Heat-flux positivity and monotonicity of TGLF in the gradients
section: Positivity: a clip in use, a penalty in training
text:
Positivity: a clip in use, a penalty in training
A ReLU inside the network passes no gradient for points it predicts as stable, so those points stop training. We follow QLKNN’s approach instead: the output stays linear during training, and where TGLF’s flux is zero or negative the loss only penalises a prediction above a small negative margin. In use, each member’s \(Q_e\) and \(Q_i\) are clipped at zero. The particle fluxes keep their sign; inward particle flux is physical.
The cost is that TGLF’s own negative heat fluxes cannot be represented: Q <= 0 in 4.6% (MAST-U) and 5.2% (ITER) of cases for Q_e, 11.8% and 13.2% for Q_i; Q < -1 gB in 0.8% and 0.7% (Q_e) and 6.5% and 4.3% (Q_i) of cases with |Q| > 1 gB; Q_e + Q_i changes by more than 10% in 0.9% and 1.0% of casesC-104. This is ceiling K-021. TORAX converts the flux to a diffusivity and clips that at a minimum, so the coupled loop already discards negative heat fluxes.
To choose the training rule we ran short CPU trainings of the TGLF-NN network on a fifth of the v1 training data, one per rule and machine. The measure is how often the surrogate returns exactly zero where TGLF’s flux is zero or negative, on the v1 test split:



training of \(Q_e\), \(Q_i\)

Q_e 0.13 (MAST-U) and 0.17 (ITER); Q_i 0.16 and 0.20C-105


fitted to \(\max(Q, 0)\)
Q_e 0.10 (MAST-U) and 0.15 (ITER); Q_i 0.06 and 0.06C-106


stability penalty, margin 0
Q_e 0.18 (MAST-U) and 0.21 (ITER); Q_i 0.13 and 0.17C-107


stability penalty, margin 1 (adopted)
Q_e 0.28 (MAST-U) and 0.40 (ITER); Q_i 0.25 and 0.43C-108

Q_e 0.45 (MAST-U) and 0.62 (ITER); Q_i 0.48 and 0.63C-109



Fitting \(\max(Q, 0)\) does worse than clipping afterwards. A larger penalty gives more zeros but starts to zero real fluxes and costs accuracy (Q_i median relative error +0.03 (MAST-U) and +0.05 (ITER); 1.0% and 1.3% of cases with Q_i > 1 gB predicted as zeroC-111). The adopted setting costs little: Q_i median relative error +0.005 (MAST-U) and +0.009 (ITER), Q_e within ±0.004; stable/unstable agreement +0.009 and +0.016; Q > 1 gB predicted zero in 0.1% (Q_e) and 0.3% (Q_i) of such casesC-110. These are smoke runs, smaller than the production models, and are used to rank the rules, not to quote accuracy. The production variant (tglfnn_symlog_relu) is to be trained on GPUs and compared with the M3 results of entry 18.

title: Heat-flux positivity and monotonicity of TGLF in the gradients
text:
Monotonicity: measured on TGLF first
We scanned TGLF directly. Per machine, 35 points from the v1 test split with both heat fluxes above 1 gB were each scanned over \(a/L_{T_e}\) and over \(a/L_{T_i}\), all other inputs fixed: 560 cases per machine, all completed; the 70 re-run base cases per machine reproduce the dataset’s fluxes bit for bitC-112. TGLF is deterministic here, so any fall in the flux along a scan is TGLF’s behaviour, not noise. The flux falls below its running maximum along most scans: falls somewhere in 77% (Q_e) and 80% (Q_i) of MAST-U scans, 51% and 74% of ITER scans; by more than half in 40% and 57% (MAST-U), 34% and 57% (ITER)C-113. The v1 ensemble, evaluated on the same scans, falls less often (falls somewhere in 20% (Q_e) and 49% (Q_i) of MAST-U scans, 23% and 37% of ITER scans; by more than half in 3% and 23% (MAST-U), 9% and 17% (ITER)C-114), and its slope is negative at a minority of test points (Q_e 8% (MAST-U) and 11% (ITER); Q_i 25% and 22%C-115). The ensemble is smoother than TGLF, so its non-monotone regions are not the same as TGLF’s.
We have not established why TGLF falls along these scans: whether the drops are changes of the dominant mode, or come from scanning one input with the others fixed, is not measured.

title: Heat-flux positivity and monotonicity of TGLF in the gradients
text:
Decision OQ-20
The owner was asked whether to drop monotonicity as a requirement, since TGLF does not satisfy it on these points. The decision (OQ-20, 1): monotonicity stays a requirement for the TGLF surrogates, \(Q_e\) non-decreasing in \(a/L_{T_e}\) and \(Q_i\) non-decreasing in \(a/L_{T_i}\). Where TGLF decreases, the surrogate departs from TGLF by construction, and that departure is to be measured and reported as a ceiling. The same decision widened the ITER collisionality range for dataset v3 (OQ-20, 2).
M3 is in progress: the production ReLU variants, the monotone surrogate and the measured departure from TGLF are next.

title: Baseline TGLF surrogates for MAST-U and ITER, including a recreated TGLF-NN
text:
new component Entry 18 · milestone M3
M2 closed on 3 October with its three acceptance criteria met (M2 page); active learning moved into M3 (OQ-18). M3 trains the surrogates: neural networks that return TGLF’s turbulent fluxes from TGLF’s local inputs, fast enough to call at every radius and time step (see the Primer). The owner set one ensemble per machine, every TGLF case kept, and the fluxes learned in a signed-log space, \(\mathrm{sign}(Q)\ln(1+|Q|)\) with \(Q\) in gyro-Bohm units (gB), because the heat fluxes in the datasets span many orders of magnitude (K-019). The accuracy target was to be set after a first baseline.

title: Baseline TGLF surrogates for MAST-U and ITER, including a recreated TGLF-NN
text:
Two networks
The baseline is a deep ensemble of 10 multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), each with four hidden layers of 256 units, trained on the same cases and differing in initialisation and minibatch order. The members’ mean is the prediction; their spread is the uncertainty.
The owner then asked for a recreation of TGLF-NN, the neural-network version of TGLF developed at General Atomics (GA) and distributed in TurbulentTransport.jl under Apache-2.0 (Neiser et al., APS-DPP 2022). GA’s training procedure is not published; the model files are, and we read the architecture from them. Each of 20 members is a residual network of width 32: an input layer, five blocks of four dense layers with a skip connection around each block, and a linear output layer. It takes GA’s choice of inputs, including the pressure and q gradients, and standardises its outputs linearly. We train it with our loss, optimiser and data. GA’s trained weights are not used.

title: Baseline TGLF surrogates for MAST-U and ITER, including a recreated TGLF-NN
text:
Held-out errors and learning curves
Each machine’s 105 cases are split at random into training, validation and test sets (80/10/10). The test cases are used once, at the end; the error is that of the ensemble mean against TGLF, on cases with |Q| above 1 gB.

GA’s linear output scaling fails on these datasets. Standardising divides each flux by its standard deviation over the training set, and the high-flux tail sets that value: 2.5 × 105 gB (MAST-U) and 1.1 × 104 gB (ITER); the median |Q_e|, 473 and 29 gB, is 0.0019 and 0.0027 standard deviationsC-085. A squared-error loss in those units is decided by the largest cases, and the typical case is not learned. GA’s training fluxes come from measured profiles and stay in a bounded range (GA’s MAST-U model -1.5 × 104 to 5.2 × 104 gB; tglf-mastu-v1 -2.4 × 106 to 2.8 × 107 gBC-086), where the same scaling works. On signed-log targets the same network matches the MLP ensemble with about a tenth of the parameters per member (21 827 per member (TGLF-NN network) against 203 526 (MLP)C-080), and its spread covers the TGLF value more often (TGLF-NN network 0.63 (MAST-U) and 0.66 (ITER); MLP ensemble 0.54 and 0.57C-081). Neither spread is calibrated; calibration is part of M4.
Retraining on a quarter and on half of the training split gives learning curves that are still falling at 80000 cases, with slopes -0.10 (MAST-U) and -0.19 (ITER) for the TGLF-NN network; -0.07 and -0.14 for the MLPC-083. A median error of 0.30 would need, by extrapolation, about 3 × 106 cases (ITER) and about 109 (MAST-U)C-084 drawn as in the M2 datasets. Both networks give nearly the same curves, so we suspect the sampling (a uniform box, mostly far above the instability threshold) more than the network; that is not yet tested.
What checks these numbers: the test cases took no part in training or in choosing the parameters each member keeps (that used the validation set). The blog’s figure script recomputes the medians from the saved models with its own code and reproduces the stored values. The comparison with GA is not independent: the network, training code and metrics are ours, and only the architecture is GA’s.

title: Reading EC heating and current without losing their conventions
text:
new component Entry 30 · milestone M3

We need to read electron-cyclotron (EC) heating and driven current before coupling them to transport. The Primer explains this source coupling; terminology is in the Glossary. The selected reference writes profiles with different averages in centimetre–gram–second (CGS) units. Their units, radial coordinate and physical meaning must be explicit.
We added a host-side reader that preserves those distinctions. It converts units to SI, retains the native bins and reduced-boundary flag, and hashes the exact bytes read. Missing channels, ambiguous units, invalid grids and missing or nonfinite values fail explicitly. Current signs are preserved.
The reader reports volume-integrated power and area-integrated toroidal current against the corresponding reference totals. These are diagnostics: no physical acceptance tolerance has been selected. Focused checks pass in both modes: 24 focused tests pass in full and Tier-A-only modesC-151. They use synthetic output files, so they establish reader behaviour rather than reference-physics accuracy. The fixtures are constructed separately from the reader, but are not an independent physical reference. Installed-wheel checks also pass in both modes; the displayed full-suite statistics remain historical.
The transport solver expects the surface average of current dotted with magnetic field for its EC current source. The reference’s current-density profiles need an explicit field/sign and geometry conversion before coupling. Its native bins also need mapping to the transport grid. Neither conversion is inferred here.
Two upstream ITER regression decks are prepared for the owner’s baseline choice. At this reader checkpoint, no reference execution, EC labels or training are claimed. The independent ITER pedestal port still needs its branch and boundary prescription; M3 remains open. The later numerical pilot exercises the reader on freshly generated reference output.
Technical details → EC native-output boundary. Decision → OQ-21.

title: Checking a saved EC reference and retaining pilot failures
text:
new component Entry 31 · milestone M3

We need a reference-file check and a runner that retains failed cases before sampling electron-cyclotron (EC) labels. The Primer explains why surrogate data needs a defined source; terminology is in the Glossary.
We checked the EC reader against a real saved output in the upstream regression suite: 200 native bins in the saved upstream ITER EC output pass reader and accounting checksC-152. Its power and toroidal-current integrals agree with the stored totals to floating-point precision. The file identifies an older solver version. Reading it validates the boundary adapter; it does not select a project launch, establish current-solver accuracy or produce new labels. The upstream file is independent of our synthetic fixtures; its accounting check still uses our reader.
The saved case also shows why current conventions matter: parallel current is negative while toroidal and ONETWO currents are positive. Preserving the channels and their signs is necessary before defining a transport-source conversion.
The new pilot runner requires explicit input files, executable, reference/build identity, case and family IDs, lineage and wall limit. It snapshots the inputs and binary, retains logs and partial outputs, records failures, and refuses to overwrite a previous run. A timeout kills the subprocess group. Every retained regular file has content-bound provenance. A readable output remains draft data; it is not a physical acceptance result or a training dataset.
40 focused pilot, reader and Tier A checks pass in full and Tier-A-only modesC-153. Lifecycle tests use fake executables, including failed launches, nonzero exits, malformed or missing outputs, changed inputs, timeout cleanup, Tier B lineage rejection and CLI failure reporting. Historical full-suite statistics remain separate from these focused checks.
Compiler and NetCDF modules are available. The checked compiler configuration does not resolve the plotting library required by the upstream build, so that dependency or a documented executable remains needed. No reference build, solver execution or cluster job was performed at this checkpoint. The build and numerical execution follow separately. Production baseline and pedestal-boundary choices remain with the owner; the independent ITER port is unchanged. M3 remains in progress.

title: Dataset v3: TGLF inputs along TORAX trajectories
text:
new component Entry 22 · milestone M3
The version 1 datasets fill a uniform box of TGLF inputs, most of it far from the plasmas the coupled simulation produces (entry 19). OQ-19 decided that dataset v3 samples where the loop goes: TGLF inputs taken from TORAX states along simulated trajectories, one family of scenarios per machine. The accuracy target, a median relative error of 0.30 on \(Q_e\) and \(Q_i\), is measured on v3’s held-out split.

title: Dataset v3: TGLF inputs along TORAX trajectories
text:
Scenario families and states
For ITER we run three TORAX examples, the RAPTOR L-mode benchmark of M1, the ITER hybrid flat-top and the ITER current ramp-up, with heating power and density scaled up and down, and with the case’s own transport model or Bohm/gyro-Bohm. For MAST-U there is no TORAX example, so we run TORAX on FreeGSNKE MAST-U-like free-boundary equilibria: eight equilibria chosen to spread over the 42 of M2, two Bohm/gyro-Bohm strengths, two heating powers, two densities, with and without a pedestal. The profiles are simulated, not measured; no experimental data are used. Runs: 128 MAST-U runs and 39 ITER runs, all completed; 32 and 8 of them held out for the test splitC-124.
At every second output state, TORAX’s own TGLF input builder gives the TGLF inputs on every face, exactly what a TGLF-type transport model receives inside the loop. The geometry inputs then come with the profiles from the same equilibrium, jointly, which removes the combinations no equilibrium has (ceiling K-018) from v3.
A face becomes a v3 state if it lies inside the region approved for M2: the kinetic ranges, the radial window and the αMHD cap (OQ-16), with the ITER collisionality range widened for v3 by the owner (OQ-20, 2). The measured M2 geometry ranges are counted but do not exclude a state, because the geometry now comes from the equilibria themselves: MAST-U 115722 of 124032 faces (93%); ITER 68978 of 79344 (87%)C-125. Where the loop goes beyond the M2 ranges, input by input: MAST-U: triangularity shear 41%, triangularity 12.5%, q 6.5%, magnetic shear 5.6%, collisionality 5%, beta_e 2%; ITER: a/L_Te 11%, a/L_Ti 10%, triangularity shear 5%, magnetic shear 3%, T_i/T_e 2%, collisionality 1%; every other input below 2%C-126. On ITER the excluded faces are mostly steeper temperature gradients than the approved range; they are not in v3, so a surrogate trained on it does not cover them either.

title: Dataset v3: TGLF inputs along TORAX trajectories
text:
Held-out runs and perturbation
The test split is made of whole runs that training never sees. For MAST-U these are all runs on two of the eight equilibria, so the test shapes are new. Test points are the held-out states as they are, because the target is to be met on the distribution the loop produces. Training points are a quarter unperturbed states and three quarters copies of states with their kinetic inputs perturbed: temperature gradients, \(T_i/T_e\), \(\beta_e\) and collisionality multiplied by log-normal factors, the density gradient and \(Z_\mathrm{eff}\) shifted, and the flow shear, which TORAX’s TGLF-type models set to zero, drawn from its approved range in half of the copies. The geometry of a copy is never perturbed. Copies outside the region are redrawn: 90000 training points (22500 unperturbed) and 10000 test points per machine; more than 99.99% of perturbed copies fell inside the region at the first drawC-127.

title: Dataset v3: TGLF inputs along TORAX trajectories
text:
TGLF labels
The labels are complete: 90000 training cases and 10000 held-out test cases per machine, all completed with finite fluxesC-128. Their recorded cost is MAST-U: 58.03 case-hours (train), 5.45 (test); ITER: 63.43 (train), 5.62 (test)C-136; these are sums over individual cases, not elapsed job times. The audit replays the sampling from the recorded plans and saved trajectories, checks that the labelled inputs equal those points, and verifies dataset hashes. For MAST-U, the plan changed after assembly; its original hash matches the recorded commit. The versioned points are kept as produced.
M3 is in progress: the structured ensembles have been trained and scored on the completed v3 test split. Their accuracy and remaining coupled-loop checks are the next entry.

title: Conventions for the EC reference labels and the ITER pedestal boundary
text:
decision new component Entry 36 · milestone M3

Two surrogates remain for M3: electron-cyclotron (EC) heating and current drive, learned from the GENRAY ray-tracing code, and the ITER pedestal, taken from a pretrained EPED neural network (EPEDNN). Both had been selected (OQ-21), but not how their outputs become TORAX inputs. The Primer explains sources and the pedestal; terms are in the Glossary.
We wrote one recommendation per open convention, and the owner accepted all of them as written.
EC labels. The current-drive calculation stays the one in the upstream ITER deck (an adjoint method). A second method with momentum conservation is run on a few cases as a check only. Electron heating keeps GENRAY’s two channels, wave-particle and collisional, separately. The current label is GENRAY’s flux-surface average of \(j \cdot B\) divided by \(B_0\). We read the GENRAY source to find which \(B_0\) this is: the vacuum toroidal field at the geometric centre stored in the equilibrium file, which is also TORAX’s definition. TORAX’s input is the same average without the division, so the coupling multiplies by TORAX’s own \(B_0\). Current is signed positive along the plasma current. Profiles go onto TORAX’s radial coordinate by a remap that keeps the volume integral of heating and the area integral of current exact in every cell. GENRAY’s radial coordinate ends slightly inside the last closed surface, and the remap rescales it with the equilibrium’s safety-factor profile. Labels are per megawatt injected. Accuracy targets are set after a first baseline.
ITER pedestal. EPEDNN returns a total pedestal pressure and a pedestal half-width in normalised poloidal flux, for three stability models and three solutions each. We use the model with both diamagnetic corrections and its first solution, which is also the upstream default. Ion and electron temperatures are equal at the pedestal top, so the temperature is the pressure divided by the electron density plus the total ion density. The pedestal density is the prescribed one, which is also an EPEDNN input. The pedestal top lies at one minus twice the half-width in poloidal flux; the upstream source documents the width as a half width. The equilibrium maps that point to TORAX’s toroidal-flux coordinate. Where the network’s inputs leave its training box, or an output is not finite, the prescribed pedestal is used instead. MAST-U keeps its prescribed pedestal.
The pedestal conversion is now code: pure JAX, compiled and differentiable, with the fallback selected per call. On the upstream ITER example it gives pedestal pressure 0.0772 MPa, T_ped 3.59 keV at n_e,ped 7e19 m^-3, top at psi_norm 0.935C-162. The checks are partly independent: the branch selection is compared with the network’s raw output vector, the temperature and coordinate conversions with hand calculations, and the fallback with inputs outside the box. They do not test the physics of the pedestal; the network is used as selected. The EC pipeline and pedestal checks pass in both modes (19 focused checks (13 EC pipeline, 6 pedestal contract) pass in full and Tier-A-only modesC-163).
The EC conventions are applied in the labelling run of the next entry. The pedestal conversion is not yet connected to TORAX. Remaining for OQ-21: the EC accuracy targets.

title: A plan for completing M3 and starting verification
text:
decision Entry 27 · milestone M3

We have written a dependency-ordered action plan for the remaining surrogate work. It distinguishes completed local validation from performance measurements, reference choices and subsequent verification.
The local transport checks are complete: 15 gradient, JIT, fallback and discrete-balance checks pass across RAPTOR and ITER hybrid in each modeC-146. The final-model matched runtime comparison remains open because its compute run was cancelled before execution. The next performance step is to resolve that cancellation, agree a fresh bounded submission and compare the final surrogate with reference transport at matched settings. Newton profiling stays separate from the linear-solver timing comparison.
In parallel, the owner can choose the reference solvers or datasets for radio-frequency (RF) and pedestal responses. That decision must specify channels, outputs, units, criteria and Tier A fallbacks. The existing guards, grouped dataset interfaces and baseline trainer are ready for those references; no predictive RF or pedestal model is trained.
After reference selection, we label a small grouped baseline, inspect errors and physical integrals, agree accuracy targets, train ensembles and integrate them into TORAX behind guards. Gradient, balance, fallback and coupled cost checks then define completion.
M3 closes only when all its required surrogate tasks meet the accuracy, differentiable execution and speed-up criteria. Verification follows: agreed properties and trajectory tolerances, formal proofs, uncertainty calibration, reference comparisons and certification review. Local sampled checks remain distinct from those certificates.
This documentation update selects no new physics closure and submits no compute job. The build log now follows the same sequence as the internal plan.

title: Transport-surrogate validation on two scenarios
text:
measurement Entry 26 · milestone M3
The final transport surrogate now has local derivative and conservation checks on ITER hybrid as well as RAPTOR L-mode. Both use the guarded ensemble, with Bohm/gyro-Bohm transport supplying coefficients wherever the guard rejects the surrogate.

title: Transport-surrogate validation on two scenarios
text:
Derivatives and conservation
The derivative checks compare automatic differentiation with finite differences. They perturb the electron-temperature profile, require the guard to select the same faces on each side of the perturbation, and require the Newton solver to reach its fine tolerance. Forward and reverse automatic differentiation must also agree. These checks cover both the initial transport coefficients and the core temperature after coupled steps.
The loop checks require finite temperatures, density and poloidal flux. They compare the selected coefficients directly with the ensemble or fallback, then rebuild discrete energy and particle balance from the solver coefficients. The existing assertion tolerances are retained: 15 gradient, JIT, fallback and discrete-balance checks pass across RAPTOR and ITER hybrid in each modeC-146.
ITER hybrid uses an explicit Newton solver override for this validation. The existing linear-solver timing configuration remains a separate experiment. The original surrogate and final model are both checked on RAPTOR; only the final model is checked on ITER hybrid.

title: Transport-surrogate validation on two scenarios
text:
What remains open
These are short local checks using ITER ensembles. They do not measure agreement with a fresh TGLF trajectory, establish a final-model speed-up or certify an error bound. The default Newton stopping tolerance still permits derivative and balance discrepancies (K-026); tighter convergence is explicit in these tests.
The new execution reports and tested source snapshots are stored separately and bound to a validation report by hashes. Reports for unchanged test files are retained when generating site statistics; the aggregate count is not a fresh full-suite rerun.
Matched final-model timing still awaits resolution of the compute cancellation. RF and pedestal training still requires the reference-target decision in OQ-21.

title: Reviewing the comparison job and saved Newton trace
text:
bug fix Entry 28 · milestone M3

We continued the action plan by inspecting the cancelled comparison job, reviewing its runner and analysing the already saved Newton trace. The scheduler still records a root cancellation without a cause. Current node status cannot explain that earlier event. The owner or scheduler support must resolve it before a fresh submission.
The runner previously returned success for coarse-tolerance solves. Those results could enter the profile comparison despite falling short of fine convergence. Execution and comparison now reject them. New output records the host and actual CPU affinity. The batch script selects allowed CPU IDs and requests a separately timed warm-up step. Execution then starts again from the initial state. Final accepted-state guard diagnostics run after timing; they do not count fallback calls within solver iterations.
Focused checks exercise rejection and overlapping trace intervals: 11 performance-tool checks pass in full and Tier-A-only modesC-147. A bounded local smoke run also checks the host runner’s warm-up and final guard output. It supplies execution evidence, not a reference comparison or speed-up measurement.
The saved Newton trace has 72059 complete HLO events with about 5.369 s of covered trace timeC-148. Taking the union of event intervals avoids counting overlap twice, but every recorded operation still belongs to the same fused module and runtime source. That does not identify ensemble inference, geometry or Jacobian cost. The performance ceiling remains open.
A concrete bounded comparison request is ready for review after the scheduler issue is resolved. No new cluster job has been submitted. RF and pedestal reference selection remains the other prerequisite for completing M3.

title: The v3 surrogates meet the held-out target
text:
measurement negative result Entry 23 · milestone M3
Dataset v3 samples where TORAX trajectories go, with whole runs kept out of training (entry 22). The final ensembles have now been trained on the broad v1/v2 data plus v3’s training points. The monotone variants meet the owner’s held-out accuracy target on both machines: MAST-U: Q_e 17.8%, Q_i 25.2%; ITER: Q_e 7.2%, Q_i 10.8%; all meet the 30% targetC-129.
An audit loaded the saved models, checked their metadata and dataset hashes, replayed the trajectory split, and recomputed the scores. The v3 test set was never a training input. This checks the implementation’s reproducibility; it is not independent physics validation.

title: The v3 surrogates meet the held-out target
text:
Structure and its cost
Electron and ion heat fluxes are nonnegative in use. Each member is built so that its heat flux cannot fall as its own temperature gradient rises, with the other inputs fixed. Recomputed checks found no negative member slopes on the tested v1/v3 points or scan grids, and no negative neighbour differences on the scan gridsC-130. Those sampled checks support the construction; proof over the whole input domain belongs to M4.
TGLF itself is not always monotone. On the broad scans where its flux decreases, the final models depart from it: MAST-U: Q_e 3.14, Q_i 3.36; ITER: Q_e 2.51, Q_i 2.11 signed-log unitsC-131. This includes approximation error as well as the cost of imposing monotonicity. Passing the v3 median target does not remove that ceiling or establish accuracy everywhere in the training box.
Clipping also does not identify every stable point. The exact-zero rates and uncalibrated spread coverage are mean ±2 standard deviations covers Q_e/Q_i at 75.3%/74.4% (MAST-U), 85.6%/80.8% (ITER); exact-zero predictions where TGLF is nonpositive: 44.0%/47.0% (MAST-U), 52.3%/21.1% (ITER)C-137. Calibration and the guard’s uncertainty policy remain M4 work.

title: The v3 surrogates meet the held-out target
text:
Inside the loop
The comparison command now selects the final monotone v3 model explicitly. A local RAPTOR L-mode run finished with all profiles finite; no stalled or coarse-tolerance step; post-step guard rejection 33.1%; execution 1.62 s after compilationC-135. Against the saved TGLF run at the same final time, its profile differences are T_e 7.72%, T_i 9.23%, n_e 11.36%, psi 0.32%C-134. Electron and ion temperature agreement improved relative to v1; density agreement did not. This is one case, not a closed-loop bound.
The strict derivative and discrete-balance checks exposed a stopping-precision limitation: v3 derivative discrepancy about 1.8e-5 relative; peak discrete energy residual 1.11e-5 (v1) and 1.36e-6 (v3)C-140. Converging Newton more tightly, to residual_tol=1e-10, gives v1 and v3 pass: three-step derivative FD tolerance 1e-7, forward/reverse tolerance 1e-12; guard masks unchanged over the stencilC-138 and v1 and v3 pass: energy residual below 1e-6 and particle residual below 1e-10, with fine solver convergenceC-139. The original assertion limits are retained. The runner records the solver setting, and the default-tolerance limitation remains K-026.
A second execution check, on ITER hybrid, gives 50 steps to 5 s, all four profiles finite, no stalled or coarse-tolerance steps; accepted-state guard rejection 26.9%C-142. It checks coupled execution and guard behavior, without a TGLF error bound.
The completed earlier timing comparison used v1. A fresh matched v3 comparison was submitted, but the scheduler cancelled it before execution and produced no output. There is no matched v3 speed-up measurement to report. The job script is prepared for a rerun once that compute issue is resolved.
M3 remains in progress: the held-out transport target passes, while matched v3 timing, broader coupled comparisons, and the RF and pedestal surrogate tasks remain open.

title: Porting the selected ITER pedestal model to JAX
text:
new component Entry 29 · milestone M3

We need a pedestal boundary that can run inside the differentiable transport loop. The Primer explains why the boundary and core evolve together; terminology is in the Glossary.
The owner has selected an electron-cyclotron (EC) heating and current-drive reference and a pretrained pressure/width pedestal model for ITER. EC labelling and the ITER port can proceed independently. MAST-U keeps its prescribed pedestal, with predictive closure deferred; ion-cyclotron work is deferred too.
We ported the selected pedestal model to JAX. Its loader checks the exact checkpoint digest and reads numeric data without executing Julia objects. Loaded inference uses JAX only. The port preserves the model’s preprocessing, neural layers, power-law correction and pressure/width outputs. All pedestal solutions remain available; no boundary branch is selected implicitly.
The port reproduces the pinned upstream regression values: 12 upstream scalar regression values agree within relative tolerance 1e-12C-149. Focused domain, solution-selection, compilation, batch and derivative checks pass in both modes: 12 focused tests pass in full and Tier-A-only modesC-150. Derivative comparisons use an interior numerical fixture and keep its domain mask unchanged. The upstream regression values are the reference; the Julia runtime itself was not executed. These are implementation checks, with no independent physicist review of the coupled boundary.
This is a numerical port of a trained model. It does not establish agreement with full EPED or with a coupled physical trajectory. The selected single network provides no ensemble spread, so no uncertainty estimate is inferred from it.
Coupled ITER integration still needs the pedestal solution, supplied density and composition, temperature partition, and conversion from the model’s poloidal-flux width to the transport boundary. The EC reference source is staged separately. Its baseline launch and current-drive prescription remain to be selected, and its current channel needs an adapter into TORAX. No EC labels or new coupled runtime result are claimed.
M3 remains in progress. Later entries record the EC reference’s build and completed numerical pilot.

title: EC reference dataset v1 on ITER states, and a first held-out baseline
text:
measurement Entry 37 · milestone M3

The electron-cyclotron (EC) surrogate needs reference labels: heating and driven-current profiles from the GENRAY ray-tracing code, for plasma states the coupling loop visits and for the launch directions an operator would use. The Primer explains sources; terms are in the Glossary.
Sampling. The plasma states come from the same family of ITER TORAX runs as transport dataset v3: the M1 benchmark case, the ITER hybrid flat top and the ITER current ramp-up, with heating and density scaled. The saved v3 files hold transport inputs only, so we ran the family again and kept the electron temperature, electron density and effective charge. From each run we take states evenly spaced in time. Each state gets launches from two launcher families: the equatorial launcher at the upstream deck’s launch point, and an upper launcher at an approximate public position (not an ITER design value). The poloidal and toroidal angles are drawn uniformly within each family’s range. Whole TORAX runs are held out for validation and test, so no held-out state shares a trajectory with a training state.
Labelling. One GENRAY process per core ran every case on one cluster node, after the owner approved the request. Each case keeps its input deck, its output file, its logs and a record of hashes and status. The plasma equilibrium is the same for every case: the upstream deck’s ITER file. This is the largest approximation in the dataset (ceiling K-028). The highest driven currents come from early ramp-up states, which are hot and dilute and in TORAX carry only a few megaamperes, traced through an equilibrium with the full plasma current. Those labels describe no consistent plasma. The collisional heating channel is zero in every case, because the deck does not enable collisional damping.



quantity
result




cases with readable output
3120 of 3120 cases produce readable output (20 of 20 check cases); median 84.8 s of GENRAY time per caseC-164


current-drive method check (momentum-conserving against adjoint)
median 4.1% difference in driven current (range -14% to +16%), identical absorbed powerC-165


first held-out baseline
driven current RMSE 3.30 kA/MW against 13.5 kA/MW for the training mean; pointwise profile model: current-density RMSE 2.20e4 A/m^2 against 2.09e4 A/m^2 for the meanC-166



Baseline. We trained the existing response baseline, an unconstrained five-member ensemble, on the totals and, separately, on the profiles point by point. The totals are learned: the driven-current error is about a quarter of the spread of the test labels. The pointwise profile model does no better than predicting the training mean. Deposition profiles are narrow peaks whose position moves with the launch angle, and a model that predicts each radius separately does not capture that. The EC surrogate therefore needs a structured output, for example deposition centre, width and totals, the same parameters as the Gaussian fallback.
The check of the labels is partial. GENRAY’s own power and current totals agree with the integrals of its profiles, and the two current-drive methods agree to a few per cent on the larger currents. Neither is an independent physics validation; both use the same rays.
Next: the owner sets accuracy targets from this baseline (B3), a structured EC model is trained (B4), and K-028 is either lifted with one equilibrium per state or the ramp-up states are restricted.
