title: ITER hybrid equilibrium solved by JOREK from the TORAX EQDSK
text:
measurement Entry 65 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)

A JOREK stability run starts from an equilibrium that JOREK solves itself, from a boundary, a pressure profile and the poloidal current function FF′. A growth rate is only meaningful if that equilibrium matches the one it is meant to represent. We therefore solved the ITER hybrid equilibrium in JOREK from the EQDSK file that TORAX ships, and compared the safety factor q.
The route needed three changes: - JOREK’s EQDSK converter needs a spline library, which we built from source. - The converter’s spline smoothing had to be raised slightly for the fit to succeed. - The converter’s outside-separatrix pressure went negative, because this EQDSK has zero pressure at the separatrix. JOREK rejects a non-positive temperature, so the temperature file was written by the toolkit adapter instead. Inside the plasma it uses the EQDSK pressure, with a small floor outside it.
JOREK read that file back exactly. The sign conventions agree: q, the toroidal field function and the axis flux all come out with the expected signs.
The core agrees, and the edge does not yet (JOREK solving the ITER hybrid equilibrium from the TORAX EQDSK matches its safety factor q to 0.4% (median) for normalised flux 0.1-0.5, but is 3.6% high for 0.5-0.9 and 5.8% high for 0.9-0.95 (q 5.12 vs 4.67 at 0.95); plasma current 12.06 vs 11.77 MAC-216). JOREK’s plasma current and q are a few percent high towards the edge. That is too large for edge-stability work, where the result depends on edge q and current. The likely causes are not yet separated: the converter’s default boundary contour lies outside the separatrix, and the FF′ spline and taper act near the edge. The proposed next step is to use the separatrix itself as the boundary and refine the grid. Stability runs would then start only once q and current match the EQDSK within an agreed tolerance.
Where this stands: the equilibrium route works end to end. The acceptance tolerance, model, dissipation, mode numbers, instability criterion and compute envelope for the first stability scans await the owner (OQ-39).

title: JOREK integration: scope, build and regression checks
text:
decision new component Entry 63 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)

JOREK is a nonlinear extended magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code for edge-localised modes (ELMs), disruptions and tearing modes in realistic X-point geometry. The toolkit’s transport loop has no MHD stability model: its pedestal is prescribed or predicted by EPEDNN, and the sawtooth model is a reduced trigger. JOREK has been open source since this year, so it can be used as an independent open (Tier A) reference for those parts.
The owner chose the scope (OQ-37). JOREK is an external reference code. It runs outside the JAX loop, never inside compiled code, and is never a runtime dependency of a surrogate. The first use is linear pedestal-stability scans over toroidal mode number on the ITER hybrid case, then an internal-kink check for the sawtooth model, then MAST-U. Nonlinear ELM runs are later reference runs only. Disruption studies are outside the brief.
We built JOREK from source on a CPU cluster with our own build of the MUMPS sparse solver, because the cluster’s shared JOREK libraries were not available to us. Two input changes were needed for the GNU Fortran compiler and the solver choice. Neither changes a value. As a check that does not depend on our code, we ran JOREK’s own regression cases against the reference data the JOREK team publishes (3 of 4 upstream regression cases reproduce their public reference data: MAST-U grid and equilibrium (largest difference 2.0e-5, tolerance 1e-4), MAST equilibrium with coils (1.2e-10), and one implicit tearing-mode step (4.1e-13, tolerance 1e-12); the full-MHD kink case was not run because its upstream input is out of date for this code versionC-210). One case could not be run: its input predates a consistency check in the current code, and fixing it would mean changing physics inputs.
A single one-hour CPU job then repeated the regression cases on the compute nodes and measured the cost of an implicit time step on the MAST-U X-point grid (all three regression cases pass on a 256-core AMD node; one implicit step on the MAST-U X-point grid (8050 elements, toroidal modes n = 0 and 1) takes 5.8 s at 2 ranks x 16 threads, 6.7 s at 4 x 32 and 8.1 s at 2 x 64; the whole job used 22.4 core-hoursC-211). That cost sets the size of the compute request for the stability scans.
Where this stands: build and regression checks done; physics settings for the first stability runs await the owner (OQ-39).

title: JOREK input adapter, output reader and run wrapper
text:
new component Entry 64 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)

To use JOREK as a reference, the toolkit has to write JOREK inputs from its own equilibria and profiles, read JOREK’s outputs, and run cases with a full record of what was executed. These parts are now in place as open (Tier A) code that runs without JOREK installed.
The design choice that mattered is what the adapter does not do. JOREK’s own conversion scripts mix unit conversion with physics choices: how profiles continue outside the separatrix, a default diffusivity, Spitzer resistivity, grid sizes. The toolkit adapter only converts units and writes files. Every physics setting is an explicit input from the caller, with no default, so each one is visible and goes to the owner for a decision.
The adapter converts to JOREK’s normalised units using the constants of the pinned JOREK version. Checked against the units JOREK itself stored in three restart files, the conversion agrees to round-off (time and resistivity units computed by the toolkit match the values JOREK stored in three restart files to 1e-15 relativeC-213). The namelist writer was tested against the real program. A MAST-U input parsed and rewritten by the toolkit gives a restart file identical to the original input’s (the MAST-U input (356 entries) parsed and rewritten by the toolkit gives, with one thread, a restart file identical in every dataset to a run of the original inputC-214). This check is independent of our code, because JOREK parses the file.
The same test exposed a property of JOREK we had to account for. Runs with more than one OpenMP thread are not bitwise repeatable, and they intermittently abort during grid set-up (an assertion in the element search tree aborts 3 of 8 grid set-up runs at 8 OpenMP threads and 0 of 8 at 1 thread; two 4-thread runs of the same input differ at round-off, while 1-thread runs repeat bit for bitC-212). The run wrapper therefore does three things: - it records ranks and threads, and marks a run as bitwise repeatable only at one thread; - it retries the grid-set-up abort once, and only when no time step has completed; - it keeps every attempt.
The wrapper snapshots the executable and inputs read-only and writes a provenance record beside every file. Its tests use fake executables (26 tests pass in normal and Tier-A-only modes: unit conversion, profile files, namelists, the energy reader, and the runner with fake executables (snapshots, retry, timeout, provenance)C-215). On the real program it reproduces a manual run exactly.
Where this stands: adapter and wrapper done; the abort is to be reported to the JOREK developers.

text:
decision measurement Entry 71 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)
Case (b) is the physical case of the JOREK stability work: the TORAX ITER hybrid state at the end of its ramp-up simulation, whose pedestal comes from the toolkit’s own pedestal model. JOREK solves its own equilibrium from the pressure, taken from TORAX’s density and temperatures, and from FF′, derived from TORAX’s current density with the bootstrap current included.

title: JOREK equilibrium for the TORAX ITER hybrid state
text:
Why the tolerance changed
The first solve missed the tolerance of entry 67: plasma current I_p came out high (first row of the table below), and so did core q. The cause is structural. TORAX evolves the current on a fixed geometry taken from the CHEASE EQDSK, so its state is not itself a Grad–Shafranov equilibrium. An equilibrium with the same pressure and current density has different flux surfaces, and therefore different q.
The owner chose the recommended option of OQ-40. FF′ is multiplied by one factor so that I_p equals TORAX’s. Acceptance is entry 67’s current tolerance, with the pressure as a function of normalised flux equal to TORAX’s by construction. The q difference from TORAX is reported, not tested. This keeps TORAX’s pressure pedestal and the shape of its current profile, which drive the edge modes. The alternatives were to tune FF′ until q matched, which changes the current profile, or to build a self-consistent free-boundary state first, which is a larger piece of work.

title: JOREK equilibrium for the TORAX ITER hybrid state
text:
What happened
The Grad–Shafranov iteration did not converge as first set up. Without under-relaxation, every case (b) solve cycles between two states, with the magnetic axis moving back and forth each iteration. This was already true of the first solve, and we didn’t flag it then. Case (b)’s FF′ is hollow, because the ramp-up current has not yet reached the core, so the axis is weakly pinned. JOREK’s under-relaxation option, which mixes each new flux half and half with the previous one, converges it.

title: Both basis roles change the reference flux
text:
measurement Entry 61 · milestone M4

The bounded diagnostic crossing the width-search basis with the final-solve basis ran once and completed. All 108 solver calls are retained, and the saved outputs pass an independent audit (2139 integrity checks pass on the complete 54-pair basis grid and all 36 consumed-control comparisons reproduce the preceding study; electron flux changes sign at every state, steps reach 4.28 gB along the final basis and 4.11 gB along the search basis, and at the largest final basis the flux is a residual of order 1e-3 gBC-205). The three settings shared with the previous study reproduce its fluxes exactly in both backends.
Neither setting explains the sensitivity on its own. Changing only the final basis moves electron heat flux by up to 4.3 gB; changing only the search basis moves it by up to 4.1 gB, and the two effects do not add. At the largest final basis tested, the flux at every state shrinks to a residual of about 1e-3 gB, which is where most negative values occur. A smaller final basis instead finds fast-growing high-wavenumber roots that carry much of the flux.
The native registers confirm the expected solver path: the search depends only on its own basis, and a final solve with no unstable mode reports the input width. They also show the search often stopping at the top of its width range.
So the reference is still not converged, and its negative values cannot yet be used. The next candidates are a larger final basis, a wider width search and tracking the high-wavenumber roots, each needing its own frozen request. The current model, guard and acceptance criteria are unchanged.

title: Linear JOREK n-scan of the ITER hybrid EQDSK case
text:
measurement bug fix Entry 68 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)
The first JOREK stability scan uses case (a): the ITER hybrid EQDSK as given, with the TORAX density used only to split its pressure into density and temperature. Each toroidal mode number n runs separately from round-off amplitude on the accepted 80 × 128 equilibrium (entry 67). The growth rate γ is the slope of ½ ln E, where E is the mode’s energy. We give γ in JOREK’s time unit √(μ₀ρ₀), about half a microsecond here.

title: Linear JOREK n-scan of the ITER hybrid EQDSK case
text:
What happened
The first job was lost. At Δt = 3 the axisymmetric start went numerically unstable, and every linear run then failed on its first step. The rerun used Δt = 1, with a health gate: the linear runs start only if the axisymmetric state keeps its equilibrium flux on axis and positive density and temperature. It passed.
Every linear run then grew over about 16 decades and stopped on JOREK’s own GMRES abort (GMRES is the iterative linear solver). JOREK exits with code 0 when this happens, so our run wrapper recorded all eight runs as completed (8 of 8 case (a) runs ended on the GMRES abort with exit code 0; a test now checks that such a run is recorded as solver_aborted and not retriedC-230). The cause: in this JOREK version a “linear” run freezes the n = 0 part, but the n ≠ 0 equations stay nonlinear, so the matrix drifts as the mode grows. The abort comes after the linear phase, so the growth data are usable. The wrapper now classifies the abort as solver_aborted, keeps the energies and does not retry, and a unit test covers it.

title: Linear JOREK n-scan of the ITER hybrid EQDSK case
text:
Growth rates
γ is fitted over the energy band 1e-15 to 1e-7, a band we chose after seeing the traces. A fit counts only if its two half-windows, and separate fits to the magnetic and kinetic energy, agree. All eight runs pass (half-window and magnetic/kinetic fits agree within 1.1% (tolerance 2%) in all 8 runs; moving the energy band one decade either way changes γ by at most 0.6%C-231).

text:
bug fix measurement Entry 67 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)
Entry 65 left JOREK’s ITER hybrid equilibrium with safety factor q and plasma current I_p a few percent high towards the edge, and the cause not yet separated. Edge-stability results depend on edge q and current, so the owner set an acceptance tolerance on q over normalised flux ψ_N 0.1–0.95 and on I_p, to be met before any stability run (OQ-39; the values are in the table).

title: ITER hybrid equilibrium in JOREK on the EQDSK separatrix
text:
Cause and fix
The TORAX ITER hybrid EQDSK comes from a fixed-boundary CHEASE solve. Its R–Z grid contains no X-point: the poloidal-flux gradient has no zero inside it. JOREK’s EQDSK converter nevertheless traces a default ITER boundary contour outside the plasma, and most of that contour lay outside the EQDSK grid. The flux there was extrapolated, and JOREK built an X-point and a separatrix of its own. The plasma it solved for was therefore not the EQDSK’s plasma.
We replaced that contour with the EQDSK separatrix itself: 300 points on the boundary flux surface, a fixed-boundary JOREK equilibrium without an X-point, on a polar flux-aligned grid. Pressure and FF′ are unchanged from entry 65.

q now matches the EQDSK across ψ_N 0.1–0.95 on every grid, more closely at the edge than in the core, so the edge mismatch of entry 65 came from the boundary. The largest q difference is the same on all three grids; only the current deficit shrinks with resolution. The check compares JOREK’s q and I_p, which JOREK computes from the boundary, pressure and FF′, with the EQDSK’s own q and I_p, which JOREK does not read. The comparison script is ours, and so is the input generator, so the check is not independent of the author. C-216 is superseded by C-221.
This boundary has a known limitation. A fixed boundary on the separatrix acts as an ideal conducting wall there, with no vacuum region outside the plasma. That stabilises peeling modes artificially. Every growth rate in the following entries carries this limitation.
The owner accepted the rest of OQ-39 as recommended: - JOREK’s model303 (reduced MHD with parallel flow and one temperature) with diamagnetic terms; - Spitzer resistivity and viscosity at Prandtl number 1; - one toroidal mode number per run, n = 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 16, 20; - a mode counts as unstable if its growth rate γ is positive with diamagnetic terms included; - γ is quoted only if halving the time step Δt and doubling the grid each leave it within a fixed tolerance (entry 69); - up to three one-node jobs.
The 80 × 128 grid is used for the scans and 160 × 256 for the grid check.
Where this stands: the equilibrium for case (a), the EQDSK as given, is accepted, and the first stability scan follows (entry 68).

title: The width-search range controls the reference flux
text:
measurement Entry 62 · milestone M4

The owner chose more numerical refinement before deciding how the MAST-U reference should treat its small negative heat fluxes. One bounded diagnostic extended the final basis to 16 functions and widened TGLF’s width search. It completed, and its saved outputs pass an independent audit with all controls reproduced (3029 integrity checks pass on the complete 78-pair extension and all 36 control comparisons reproduce job 2687308; NBASIS_MAX 16 still moves electron flux by up to 0.48 gB per step, and widening the width search from 1.65 to 3.3 changes it from about 1e-3 gB to as much as 181 gBC-206).
Neither change settles the flux. The near-zero values seen at the previous largest basis disappear again at larger bases, and the last step still moves the electron flux by up to 0.48 gB. Widening the width search matters far more: the default range turns out to be binding, and letting the search move past it turns a residual of about 1e-3 gB into as much as 181 gB at one state. At the standard settings, the two negative values become clearly positive.
Across three bounded studies the “refined” flux at these states spans more than five orders of magnitude. The standard settings, which labelled all the training data, therefore act as a convention that defines the model here rather than as an approximation to a converged answer. How to use that convention for the reference goes back to the owner. The current model, guard and acceptance criteria are unchanged.

title: A full-precision signed-heat diagnostic route is prepared
text:
new component Entry 54 · milestone M4

The current in-memory trapped gyro-Landau fluid (TGLF) wrapper returns integrated fluxes but does not expose mode spectra. The next diagnostic therefore uses an original driver linked to the installed solver library. It writes signed heat flux separately for electrons, main ions and impurities, plus low-k totals, eigenvalues and heat spectra by field, wavenumber and mode at full precision.

title: Owner limits the MAST-U certification scope
text:
decision measurement Entry 70 · milestone M4
M4’s closed-loop check runs the coupled simulation once with the transport surrogate and once with TGLF, the turbulence code it was trained on, and compares the temperature profiles. The limit is 15%. ITER passes (served-face T_e 7.42%, T_i 8.18%, both passing the 15% limit; whole profile 7.72/9.23%; 34 of 51 final-state faces servedC-178) and MAST-U fails (served-face T_e 35.33%, T_i 49.15%, both failing 15%; whole profile 41.51/62.39%; cells with both adjacent faces served give 11.86/23.24%, still failing T_i; 13 of 26 final-state faces servedC-179). The MAST-U remediation retrained the surrogate. It then stopped at the step that needs a TGLF reference trajectory to compare the retrained candidate with. At some MAST-U states TGLF returns negative heat diffusivities, which the guard rejects, so those faces of the reference use the fallback transport model instead. Refining TGLF’s numerical settings did not converge those values (entries 59–62, last entry 62).

title: Owner limits the MAST-U certification scope
text:
The projected reference
For the reference only, the owner chose TGLF at its standard settings with every negative heat diffusivity set to zero, each projection logged, and a stop if any projected heat flux reaches 1 gB (the gyro-Bohm flux unit) (OQ-38). The production surrogate and guard were unchanged. The single approved run stopped on that limit and saved no trajectory.
To see whether a rerun could pass, we applied the same rule, read-only, to every face of the 40 saved states of the earlier unprojected reference run, which has identical profiles:

26 would be served, the first at state 4 (faces 11 and 12, ion, −8.0 and −33.8 gB); near the axis the projected magnitude reaches 6020 gBC-241

The stop applies to every projection, served or not, and the first one to reach it comes at state 1 (first table row). So the rule cannot complete on this scenario, and no rerun can produce the reference. Even counting only served faces, it would stop early. title: Owner limits the MAST-U certification scope
text:
Decision
The owner chose the recommended option of OQ-42, limited MAST-U scope: - the MAST-U closed-loop comparison is recorded as not evaluable; - MAST-U is certified at the M4 review with that limitation stated, with ceilings K-030 and K-032; - ITER’s measured pass stands; - the model, the guard, the temperature and flux acceptance limits and the frozen data splits are unchanged; - no further MAST-U reference compute is planned.

title: Verification
text:
Projected-reference stop review
OQ-38 selects the standard-settings convention and permits projecting finite negative heat diffusivities to zero in the reference only. The consumed trajectory stopped at the approved projection limit (the projected-reference job failed after 108 s when the log reported 3.93119 gB against the 1 gB stop limit; no completed reference was savedC-217). The saved exception reports a magnitude but no triggering face, state or channel. This supplies no completed reference and cannot close K-030; the convention does not lift the numerical sensitivity in K-032. OQ-42 then limited the MAST-U scope (MAST-U scope).
The original host runner accumulated projection history in memory and raised on the limit before saving it. Existing tests checked that it stopped and wrote no successful trajectory, so they missed the lost evidence. The corrected runner writes a bound projection log before enforcing the limit and saves a separate raw diagnostic snapshot on failure. Regression tests check those bytes and their provenance after the actual loop raises, with physical solver calls forbidden.
Only finite negative heat coefficients are zeroed. Both infinities and NaN remain invalid; a numerical maximum alone would incorrectly map negative infinity to zero. The saved-output audit requires full guard features and exact boolean-mask dimensions. Future acceptance also checks parent hashes and the complete frozen scenario, so individually valid sidecars cannot hide substituted inputs. These changes do not modify the selected surrogate or production guard settings.
The original failed package and missing information remain recorded. No repeated reference run or recovered face identity is claimed. Draft entry 66 records the review and remains held for publication.

title: Verification
text:
Transport monotonicity
The V4 result is all 20 members of each ensemble pass both heat-flux monotonicity properties, with derivative lower bound zero over the full training boxC-247. Draft narrative entry 74 accompanies this technical account and remains pending publication. The result proves an imposed network property, with the K-025 physical-model departure caveat retained.
For one constrained head, write its derivative as
\[
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial g}
= \frac{s_y}{s_x} W_{out} D_L W_L \cdots D_0 w_g.
\]
The gradient coordinate is excluded from the free trunk and from its own head’s free input vector. The effective constrained weights are absolute values of saved parameters; all normalization scales are positive. For ELU, the derivative is \(\exp(\min(z,0))\); for reflected ELU it is \(\exp(\min(-z,0))\); for the saturated mix it is \(\exp(-\max(|z|-1,0))\). Every derivative lies in \([0,1]\).
The structural route checks the saved routing, finite parameters, scales and supported transforms. The second route exports the derivative product itself and uses auto_LiRPA interval bound propagation over independent diagonal entries in \([0,1]\). This enlarged slope domain contains the image of the entire raw-input box; no box shrinking or input split is required. The result is a non-negative derivative before the output ReLU. The positive affine maps, ReLU, inverse signed-log transform and mean preserve monotonicity through serving.
Each export and derivative graph is checked against JAX before the corresponding proof, on random-box and original held-out points, under OQ-26. These numerical comparisons validate the implementation path; the domain-wide result comes from the structural and interval arguments. The certificates cover real-valued functions represented by the saved parameters, not directed-rounding guarantees for every floating-point execution.
Certificates retain individual member/pair bounds, model and box hashes, verifier versions and source digests. V4 is complete for the two baseline transport ensembles. Physical reference admissibility, output bounds, conformal calibration, production guard binding, CI re-proofs and the final certification review remain separate obligations.

title: Verification
text:
Output bounds
V5 now has an executable CROWN calculation and complete input splitting. The verifier first checks each proof export against JAX on random box points and the original held-out inputs. Transport’s input logarithms map interval endpoints monotonically. Its signed-log inverse is applied only after bounding the training-space output. EC fixes the launcher indicator to one family at a time while retaining every other stored input range, then applies the serving clamps to each member’s interval.
The proof graph expresses ELU as
\[\operatorname{ELU}(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(x)
  +\exp(-\operatorname{ReLU}(-x))-1.\]
The saturated monotone-head activation uses the equivalent expression
\[\operatorname{clip}(x,-1,1)
+\exp(-\operatorname{ReLU}(-x-1))
-\exp(-\operatorname{ReLU}(x-1)).\]
These identities avoid unsupported export operators. They preserve the real-valued function, but the separate relaxations can be loose; passing parity does not guarantee useful bounds. The retained certificate names the float64 calculation and does not claim directed-rounding verification of IEEE execution.
Each split bisects the largest side relative to the original box. A parent is replaced only after both children have bounds. Child intervals are intersected with their parent, and the final interval is the minimum lower and maximum upper bound across all retained leaves. The leaf and time budgets are explicit. The time budget is checked between bound calls; the execution wrapper supplies the hard process limit. Sampled extrema measure the interval’s tightness and must lie inside it; samples never supply the proof.
For the pedestal, the diagnostic now saves the upstream input vector at every retained output state, its feature names and model hash. The proof box encloses those vectors, widened by a declared fraction of the upstream range on each axis. Any clipping of that margin at the upstream domain is recorded; a visited point outside the upstream domain fails. The upstream box alone cannot replace a missing trajectory. CROWN bounds the neural residual; interval composition adds the power law, squares each solution and multiplies each pressure by the positive density interval. All pressure and half-width solutions remain explicit, including the GH solution used by TORAX.
Reports bind the model, property, boxes, datasets, producing source and verifier library. A nonfinite physical interval is recorded as unknown. Such a row supplies no guard domain; V10 integration requires usable certified bounds and the owner’s fallback-rate threshold.

title: Verification
text:
Conformal calibration
V7 is complete for the three labelled surrogates (90% intervals calibrated on the v1 validation split cover 0.887–0.907 on the v1 test and v2-random splits (6 outputs, ITER and MAST-U); 9 of 12 lie in the 0.893–0.907 range expected for exchangeable data, the other three miss it by at most 0.006C-256, the same intervals cover 0.996–1.000 of the v3 test states; there the half-width that would give 90% is 3.3–5.5 times smaller in signed-log units (ITER Q_e 0.48 against 2.21)C-257, 90% intervals calibrated on 190 guard-accepted validation states (4 runs) cover 0.876–0.978 of 548 served test states (8 runs); all six outputs lie within or above the 0.856–0.938 range expected for exchangeable data; per-run coverage 0.78–1.00C-258). Draft entry 76 is the narrative account.
For each served output, with prediction \(\hat y\) and label \(y\) on \(n\) calibration points, the score is \(s_i = |y_i - \hat y_i|\). The half-width is the \(k\)-th smallest score, with \(k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil\) and \(\alpha = 0.1\). The interval is \([\hat y - q, \hat y + q]\). If calibration and test points are exchangeable, the interval covers a new label with probability at least \(1-\alpha\). The probability is marginal, over both the calibration draw and the new point. MAPIE’s prefit SplitConformalRegressor computes \(q\), and the code checks each value against the exact rank.
The prediction is the one each guard serves. - Transport. The prediction is the members’ mean in training space, \(t = \operatorname{sign}(Q)\log(1 + |Q|)\). The score is taken in \(t\), and the physical interval is the inverse transform of \([\hat t - q, \hat t + q]\). The transform is increasing, so coverage is the same in both spaces. A half-width \(q\) spans a factor \(e^{q}\) on \(1 + |Q|\). - EC. The prediction is the bounded per-MW output. Only states that the EC source’s guard would accept count: padded box, finite outputs, and member spreads within the source defaults. Transport counts only points inside its training box.
Calibration uses the split recorded with each model, which also chose each member’s early-stopping epoch. Test coverage is the evidence. For \(m\) test points, the number covered under exchangeability is beta-binomial with parameters \((m, k, n+1-k)\). Its central 90% range, which includes both random draws, is stored beside each coverage. Before calibrating, the code re-scores every split and must match the model’s stored RMSE to \(10^{-4}\); the match was exact.
The results, stored per surrogate: - Transport, data drawn like the calibration split. Coverage is close to 0.9. - Transport, held-out TORAX trajectory states. Coverage is 0.996–1.000. The half-widths that would give 90% there are 3.3–5.5 times smaller. Whether to add a loop-state calibration for M5 awaits an owner decision. - Transport, by flux size. The score is uniform in \(t\), so coverage is lower where \(|Q| > 1\) gB (0.86–0.90 on v1 test) and higher below it. - EC. Pooled coverage of the 548 served states from eight held-out runs is 0.876–0.978. Per run it ranges from 0.78 to 1.00. Within a run, states are correlated. - Pedestal. EPEDNN has no labelled data here, so it has no interval.
Records bind the model and manifest hashes through provenance sidecars. Readers obtain them through load_record, which refuses a record whose model hash differs.

Loop-state calibration (OQ-44)
The owner chose a second transport calibration on the states the coupled runs visit, for M5 (calibrated on half of the held-out v3 trajectory runs, the 90% half-widths are 0.21–0.32 of the V7 values; the intervals span a factor 1.8–3.3 on 1 + |flux| instead of 9–60C-259, calibrated on 16 held-out runs and tested on the other 16, coverage is 0.870–0.894; the reverse direction gives 0.905–0.924; single runs 0.75–0.97C-260, calibrated on 4 held-out runs, the intervals cover 0.936–0.966 of the other 4; calibrated the other way they cover 0.711–0.818; not reliable for a new ITER runC-261). Draft entry 77 is the narrative account. The V7 records above remain the M4 deliverable.
The held-out v3 test runs are whole TORAX trajectories: eight for ITER and 32 for MAST-U. The split rule was committed before any residual on these states was computed: - group the runs by scenario family (ITER) or equilibrium (MAST-U); - permute each group’s runs with a fixed seed; - deal the runs alternately to half A (calibration) and half B (report); - drop states shared by runs in both halves (common start-up states).
The method is otherwise the V7 one. The reverse direction, calibrating on B and reporting on A, tests whether runs are exchangeable.
The half-widths fall to 0.21–0.32 of the box-wide values. For MAST-U, coverage of the other half is 0.870–0.894, and 0.905–0.924 in reverse; single runs range from 0.75 to 0.97. For ITER, coverage of B is 0.936–0.966, but only 0.711–0.818 in reverse. The marginal guarantee assumes that calibration and test points are exchangeable. With four runs per half and systematic differences between runs, that assumption fails for ITER. A calibration that treats runs as the unit needs more held-out trajectories than the eight available.

title: Linear JOREK n-scan of the TORAX ITER hybrid state: three pedestal modes grow
text:
measurement Entry 73 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)
The first case (b) job (entry 72) ended before most modes had grown far enough to measure. The second job continued every toroidal mode number n from its own last saved time slice, with unchanged inputs. The rule for fitting the growth rate γ was fixed before this job’s data were analysed: fit ½ ln E from 4 to 10 decades above the run’s minimum energy, require the two halves of the window and the magnetic and kinetic energies to give the same γ (the agreement test used for case (a)), and read the location from the flow perturbation.

title: Linear JOREK n-scan of the TORAX ITER hybrid state: three pedestal modes grow
text:
What happened
All eight runs reached the time limit without a solver abort. Below n = 12 nothing grew measurably (the continuation job ran all eight n to its time limit (t ≈ 9470–9670) with no solver abort; n = 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 show no measurable growth by t ≈ 9671 (under 6 decades above their minimum energy)C-243). The three highest n grew cleanly, all in the pedestal:



n
γ√(μ₀ρ₀) and location




12, 16, 20
γ√(μ₀ρ₀) = 0.00218 (n = 12), 0.00192 (n = 16) and 0.00288 (n = 20), all with the flow perturbation peaked at ψ_N 0.925–0.975; fits over 2400–3400 points, half-window and magnetic/kinetic fits agreeing within 0.6%, and shifting the fit band by a decade changes γ by under 1e-4C-244



By the criterion the owner chose (γ > 0 with diamagnetic terms included), these three modes are unstable. They are weak: about 15 times slower than case (a)’s pedestal modes, and far below the EPED-like threshold on the ratio of γ to the ion diamagnetic frequency (γ/ωᵢ = 0.054 (n = 12), 0.036 (n = 16), 0.043 (n = 20), against the EPED-like threshold 0.25; ωᵢ is an estimate from the profiles, not a JOREK outputC-245). γ is not monotone in n.
One point on process. The window rule was fixed in the plan before any data from this job were read. While the job was still running, we looked once at interim output with the old case (a) rule. The code for the new rule was then written by a session that had not seen the data.

title: Linear JOREK n-scan of the TORAX ITER hybrid state: three pedestal modes grow
text:
What is not yet checked
These growth rates are not converged. Decision 7 asks that halving the time step and doubling the grid each leave γ within the agreed tolerance. The time-step check is running now: each of the three modes restarts twice from the same saved slice, at Δt = 1 and Δt = 0.5. The slice is the first one inside its fit window. The same job also prepares the doubled grid’s axisymmetric state.
The grid check is the hard part. These modes take thousands of time units to rise from round-off, and JOREK in this version cannot start the fine grid from the coarse mode. A from-scratch check on the doubled grid would take many more jobs than remain (repeating the slow emergence (4 decades only by t ≈ 4700–6900) plus a fit window on 160 × 256 means about 7000–9000 steps per mode, about 60–190 h at an estimated 30–75 s per step, so 10–32 chained jobs for the three modes run togetherC-246). The recommendation to the owner (OQ-43) is to measure the grid sensitivity on case (a)’s faster pedestal modes instead, and to report case (b) as converged in time step only.

title: Time-step check of the case (b) pedestal growth rates
text:
measurement Entry 75 · milestone JOREK (alongside M4)
Entry 73 found three toroidal mode numbers of the TORAX ITER hybrid state growing at the pedestal: n = 12, 16 and 20. Decision 7 asks that a growth rate γ change by no more than the agreed tolerance when the time step is halved and when the grid is doubled. This entry is the time-step half of that check.

title: Time-step check of the case (b) pedestal growth rates
text:
Method
Repeating the slow rise from round-off at half the time step would have cost several jobs. We therefore restarted each mode twice from the same saved state, once at Δt = 1 and once at Δt = 0.5, and fitted both runs over the same window. All three rules were fixed before the job ran, with every input recorded by checksum: - which modes to restart: those growing in entry 73; - which saved state: the first one inside each mode’s fit window; - how to compare the runs.

title: Time-step check of the case (b) pedestal growth rates
text:
What happened
All six runs reached the time limit with no solver abort. Halving the time step changed γ by at most about one part in ten thousand, and every mode stayed at the pedestal (restarting n = 12, 16 and 20 from the same saved state at Δt = 1 and Δt = 0.5 changes γ by 1.3e-5, 9.6e-5 and 7.9e-5, against the 5% tolerance of decision 7; the location stays at the pedestal in both runsC-248). As a control, the Δt = 1 restarts reproduce the original job’s growth rates almost exactly (the Δt = 1 restarts reproduce the original job’s growth rate over the shared window to 9e-10–3e-8C-249). The case (b) pedestal growth rates are therefore converged in time step (γ√(μ₀ρ₀) = 0.00218 (n = 12), 0.00192 (n = 16) and 0.00288 (n = 20), flow perturbation peaked at ψ_N 0.925–0.975; converged in time step (C-248)C-251).
The same job used its spare cores to run the axisymmetric start of case (b) on the doubled grid. It passed its health check and is kept as the starting state for a grid check (50 axisymmetric steps on the 160 × 256 grid in 40 min on 64 cores; the state passed its health check and is kept as the start for a grid checkC-250).

text:

The grid check. On the doubled grid these modes would again have to rise from round-off, which takes many jobs, and JOREK in this version cannot start the fine grid from the coarse mode. The owner’s decision on how to proceed is pending (OQ-43). title: Bounding the Unpredictable
text:
If a neural network’s input can move anywhere within a known set, how far can its output move?
Neural surrogates now stand in for expensive simulations, including in fusion plasma modelling. There, a single prediction is not enough; we need to know where the output can go. Sampling inputs estimates that range but cannot prove it is complete. A verified enclosure can, provided it is tight enough to use.
The cheapest enclosure is loose. Rather than survey every tighter method, we diagnose one source of looseness at a time and address it. Each section follows the same loop:
The examples move up in complexity: a scalar function, then a small ReLU network, then an attention head.
A more elaborate method is not automatically a tighter one. Three times below — the centred form, the degree-two Taylor model and fixed-slope CROWN — the more sophisticated choice gives a bound no tighter than the simpler one. Each failure sharpens the diagnosis.
Derivations and supplementary experiments sit in the collapsible sections. Code and reproduction instructions · Verification and limitations

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: What counts as a good bound
text:
What counts as a good bound
Consider a fixed network \(f\) and a set of possible inputs \(\mathcal X\). We seek two numbers such that
\[
\boxed{L\le f(x)\le U\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal X.}
\]
A bound is sound if it contains every possible output and tight if it leaves little extra room. Soundness is non-negotiable; tightness costs computation.
A fair comparison fixes the function, the input set and the output being bounded, and reports the width \(U-L\) alongside the computational work. Widening the input set changes the problem, not the method. Samples can expose an unsound bound but cannot certify a sound one.

About the experiments: the formulas assume real arithmetic. Browser rounding is not validated, so the numerical results are illustrative, not machine-verified certificates.



Mathematics: exact ranges and validated arithmetic

For a scalar output, define
\[
y_{\min}=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x),\qquad
y_{\max}=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x).
\]
We seek \(L\le y_{\min}\le y_{\max}\le U\). A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains both extrema. For vector outputs, these inequalities apply componentwise; an output box can still lose relationships between components.
Validated arithmetic makes the mathematical inclusion survive computation: round lower endpoints down and upper endpoints up, including errors in coefficients, transcendental functions and optimisation results. This establishes soundness; it does not itself remove dependency overestimation. Adding an arbitrary small epsilon is not a proof. Here, binary64 arithmetic is unvalidated and every result has certified: false; finite tests diagnose errors but cannot prove a continuum claim.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
text:
Intervals forget shared variables
We start with the simplest case that exposes the main failure. Consider
\[
f(x)=x(1-x),\qquad x\in[0,1].
\]
The maximum lies at \(x=1/2\), so the exact range is \([0,1/4]\).
Baseline. Interval arithmetic bounds each operation independently: \(x\in[0,1]\) and \(1-x\in[0,1]\), so their product lies in \([0,1]\). The bound is sound but four times wider than the true range.
Diagnosis. Both factors depend on the same \(x\), so they cannot both equal one. Interval arithmetic discards this. The expression \(x-x\) isolates the failure: interval subtraction returns \([-1,1]\) for a quantity that is always zero.
Intervention. By rewriting the expression so that \(x\) appears once, we restore the lost relationship. Completing the square gives
\[
x(1-x)=\frac14-(x-\tfrac12)^2,
\]
and interval arithmetic now returns the exact range \([0,1/4]\).
A plausible intervention that fails. The centred (mean-value) form at \(c=1/2\) adds derivative information but returns \(1/4+[-1,1][-1/2,1/2]=[-1/4,3/4]\) — the same width as the baseline, with neither interval containing the other. Extra information helps only when the calculation exploits it.
The experiment below compares equivalent expressions and subdivided intervals.
Compare equivalent expressions and subdivided intervals. Enable JavaScript to use the controls.


Derivation: interval arithmetic, centred / mean-value forms, and IBP

Classical interval arithmetic bounds each operation over a rectangle. For \(X=[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(Y=[\ell_y,u_y]\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
X+Y&=[\ell_x+\ell_y,u_x+u_y],\\
X-Y&=[\ell_x-u_y,u_x-\ell_y],\\
XY&=[\min S,\max S],\\
S&=\{\ell_x\ell_y,\ell_xu_y,u_x\ell_y,u_xu_y\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
A bilinear function reaches its extrema over a rectangle at corners. The enclosure is exact for independent operands; repeated occurrences of the same variable may not be independent. If \(0\notin Y\), \(1/Y=[1/u_y,1/\ell_y]\); division across zero is rejected here. A dedicated square operation preserves repetition:
\[
X^2=\begin{cases}
[0,\max(\ell_x^2,u_x^2)],&\ell_x\le0\le u_x,\\
[\min(\ell_x^2,u_x^2),\max(\ell_x^2,u_x^2)],&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Centred / mean-value forms use derivative information to avoid repeatedly expanding the original expression. For \(c\in X\) and a differentiable \(f\), let \(F'(X)\) enclose every derivative on \(X\). The mean-value theorem gives
\[
f(X)\subseteq f(c)+F'(X)(X-c).
\]
For \(f(x)=x(1-x)\), \(F'(X)=1-2X\). This can tighten a natural interval expression, but is not always tighter: the derivative enclosure can itself be loose. Intersecting two sound enclosures retains their stronger information.
Interval bound propagation (IBP) applies these rules layer by layer. For \(z=Wx+b\), write \(W^+=\max(W,0)\) and \(W^-=\min(W,0)\) elementwise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underline z&=W^+\underline x+W^-\overline x+b,\\
\overline z&=W^+\overline x+W^-\underline x+b.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each coefficient selects the endpoint that minimises or maximises its contribution. Increasing activations then use \([\sigma(\underline z),\sigma(\overline z)]\); nonmonotone activations require interior extrema too. IBP is inexpensive and supplies useful pre-activation bounds for stronger methods, but replacing each layer by a box loses dependence.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
text:
Affine arithmetic keeps shared variables
Inside a network, a convenient rewrite is rarely available, so we track shared variables explicitly. Affine arithmetic represents each uncertain quantity as
\[
x=x_0+\sum_i a_i\epsilon_i,\qquad \epsilon_i\in[-1,1].
\]
By reusing the same noise symbols \(\epsilon_i\) in every quantity derived from \(x\), affine arithmetic preserves linear dependence: \(x-x\) cancels exactly. With several outputs, the represented set is a zonotope. Linear layers map zonotopes to zonotopes exactly. Affine arithmetic
Limitation. Each nonlinear operation introduces a fresh error symbol, independent of all others. Across repeated nonlinear layers these accumulate and erode the benefit. Constrained zonotopes exclude infeasible combinations of symbols; polynomial zonotopes retain the nonlinear terms. Both trade computation for retained information.
The interval-versus-affine experiment closes the derivation below.


Derivation: affine arithmetic, zonotopes, constrained and polynomial zonotopes

Affine arithmetic keeps shared noise symbols. For \(\hat x=x_0+\sum_i a_i\epsilon_i\) and \(\hat y=y_0+\sum_i b_i\epsilon_i\),
\[
\hat x+\hat y=x_0+y_0+\sum_i(a_i+b_i)\epsilon_i,
\qquad \lambda\hat x=\lambda x_0+\sum_i\lambda a_i\epsilon_i.
\]
This preserves cancellation across linear operations. Let \(\delta_x=\hat x-x_0\), \(r_x=\sum_i|a_i|\), and similarly for \(y\). Multiplication gives
\[
\hat x\hat y=x_0y_0+\sum_i(x_0b_i+y_0a_i)\epsilon_i+\delta_x\delta_y.
\]
Since \(|\delta_x\delta_y|\le r_xr_y\), replace the last term by \(r_xr_y\epsilon_{\rm new}\). For a square, the stronger \(\delta_x^2\in[0,r_x^2]\) permits the residual \(r_x^2/2+(r_x^2/2)\epsilon_{\rm new}\). Fresh residual symbols cost storage and lose nonlinear dependence; repeated nonlinear layers can accumulate this error.
Zonotopes collect affine forms into a vector set:
\[
\mathcal Z=\{c+G\epsilon:\|\epsilon\|_\infty\le1\},\qquad
W\mathcal Z+b=\{Wc+b+WG\epsilon:\|\epsilon\|_\infty\le1\}.
\]
Affine maps are exact in this representation. Rotating a rectangle therefore preserves its tilted shape, while an axis-aligned box includes extra space. Affine arithmetic and zonotope propagation share one implementation in the network comparison.
Constrained zonotopes retain additional feasible relationships:
\[
\mathcal Z_c=\{c+G\epsilon:\|\epsilon\|_\infty\le1,\ A\epsilon=d\}.
\]
The constraints exclude combinations of factors that cannot occur, potentially tightening ranges at the cost of constrained optimisation. The demo’s \(\epsilon_2=\epsilon_1\) can be eliminated analytically; general coordinate bounds can require LP. Constrained zonotopes
Polynomial zonotopes retain shared higher-order factors:
\[
\mathcal P=\left\{c+\sum_i g_i\prod_j\epsilon_j^{E_{ji}}:
\epsilon_j\in[-1,1]\right\},\qquad E_{ji}\in\mathbb N_0.
\]
For \(u=a\epsilon_1+b\epsilon_2\) and \(v=c\epsilon_1+d\epsilon_2\), the quadratic map is exactly
\[
v+0.4u^2=c\epsilon_1+d\epsilon_2+0.4a^2\epsilon_1^2
+0.8ab\epsilon_1\epsilon_2+0.4b^2\epsilon_2^2.
\]
Keeping these monomials avoids immediately replacing curvature by independent noise. More terms mean more work; reductions may need independent residual factors. A polynomial zonotope describes a set, whereas a Taylor model couples a polynomial approximation to a remainder on a specified domain. Neither is simply an affine form with a different name. The demo draws an analytically parametrised boundary; its finite drawing is not a containment proof. Polynomial zonotopes
Compare interval and affine enclosures under a linear or quadratic map.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: 4. Keep the polynomial; bound what is missing
text:
4. Keep the polynomial; bound what is missing
Affine forms retain only first-order dependence. Why discard higher powers if we can afford to carry them?
For \(f\in C^{k+1}\) on the segment joining \(c\) to every point in \(X\), Taylor’s theorem states
\[
f(x)=\underbrace{\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j}_{P_k(x-c)}
+\frac{f^{(k+1)}(\xi_x)}{(k+1)!}(x-c)^{k+1}.
\]
If \(|f^{(k+1)}|\le M\) on that segment and \(h=\max_{x\in X}|x-c|\), then
\[
f(x)\in P_k(x-c)+R,\qquad
R=\left[-\frac{Mh^{k+1}}{(k+1)!},\frac{Mh^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\right].
\]
The pair \((P_k,R)\) is a Taylor model. The polynomial records how the output depends on the original variable; \(R\) covers everything omitted. For \(e^x\), use \(M=e^{\max(X\cup\{c\})}\); for \(\sin x\), use \(M=1\). A quadratic becomes exact at degree two, apart from implementation roundoff. Berz and Makino’s Taylor-model resources and the formally verified Taylor-model development by Traut and Immler describe rigorous computational treatments.

Arithmetic on models
Let \(f\in P+R\) and \(g\in Q+S\) on a common domain in the same variables. Addition gives \((P+Q)+(R+S)\). For multiplication, form the full polynomial product and split it into retained and discarded terms:
\[
PQ=T_k(PQ)+D.
\]
If \(\mathcal B(P)\) encloses the range of \(P\) on the domain, then
\[
fg\in T_k(PQ)+
\underbrace{\mathcal B(D)+\mathcal B(P)S+\mathcal B(Q)R+RS}_{\text{new remainder}}.
\]
The discarded coefficients cannot simply disappear. Even tiny coefficients may multiply large powers over a wide interval. The module used here applies this rule directly and bounds retained and discarded polynomials using Bernstein coefficients.
Composition makes the distinction concrete. For \(f(x)=\exp(x(1-x))\), set \(t=x-c\), \(q_c=c(1-c)\), and \(v=(1-2c)t-t^2\). Then
\[
f(x)=e^{q_c}\exp(v),\qquad
\exp(v)=\sum_{j=0}^k\frac{v^j}{j!}+r(v).
\]
The browser repeatedly multiplies Taylor models, retaining degree at most \(k\). If \(v(X)\subseteq[v_-,v_+]\), the final exponential series remainder satisfies
\[
|e^{q_c}r(v)|\le
\frac{e^{q_c+\max(0,v_+)}\max(|v_-|,|v_+|)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}.
\]
This is a finite composition of models with explicitly retained truncation errors, rather than a fitted curve with a sampled error bar.
Interactive experiment: Taylor polynomials and analytic remainder envelopes for a quadratic, exp(x), sin(x), and exp(x(1 − x)).
Increasing degree primarily reduces approximation and truncation error. It does not remove the true variation of \(f\), nor automatically solve the separate problem of finding a polynomial’s range. Subdivision may help both, at the cost of maintaining several models. Repeated composition can also enlarge the remainder until it dominates the polynomial information.
A polynomial zonotope writes a vector-valued polynomial image in shared factors:
\[
\mathcal P=\left\{c+\sum_i g_i\prod_j\epsilon_j^{E_{ji}}:
\epsilon_j\in[-1,1]\right\}.
\]
Integer exponents retain repeated nonlinear dependencies, as in the preceding geometry experiment. Taylor models pair polynomials with a separately bounded remainder; polynomial zonotope representations organize dependent monomials and may add independent generators for residual uncertainty. Their data structures and reduction operations differ. Kochdumper and Althoff develop sparse polynomial zonotopes for reachability.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: 5. A good approximation still needs a range bound
text:
5. A good approximation still needs a range bound
Consider a polynomial \(p\) mapped to \(t\in[0,1]\). In the Bernstein basis,
\[
p(t)=\sum_{i=0}^n b_i B_{i,n}(t),\qquad
B_{i,n}(t)=\binom ni t^i(1-t)^{n-i}.
\]
Each basis function is nonnegative, and the binomial theorem gives \(\sum_iB_{i,n}(t)=1\). The polynomial is therefore a convex combination of its coefficients:
\[
\min_i b_i\le p(t)\le\max_i b_i.
\]
To reproduce the calculation, substitute \(x=a+(b-a)t\) into a power-basis polynomial. If the resulting coefficients are \(q_k\), then
\[
b_i=\sum_{k=0}^{i}q_k\frac{\binom ik}{\binom nk}.
\]
For \(x(1-x)\) on \([0,1]\), the degree-two Bernstein coefficients are \((0,1/2,0)\), giving \([0,1/2]\). Splitting at \(1/2\) yields coefficients \((0,1/4,1/4)\) and \((1/4,1/4,0)\) on the two halves: their combined enclosure is the exact \([0,1/4]\). The unsplit bound was conservative even though there was no approximation error.

Chebyshev approximations and validation
Chebyshev polynomials satisfy \(T_k(\cos\theta)=\cos(k\theta)\). On a scaled coordinate \(t\in[-1,1]\), an interpolant takes the form
\[
p_n(t)=\sum_{k=0}^n c_kT_k(t).
\]
Using the roots of \(T_{n+1}\) distributes interpolation nodes more densely near the ends. This often gives a useful approximation over a whole interval. But an approximation alone gives no enclosure of the original function.
For the lab’s \(f(x)=e^x\) on \([a,b]\), let \(h=(b-a)/2\) and \(N=n+1\). The interpolation remainder and the leading coefficient of \(T_N\) give
\[
|f(x)-p_n(x)|\le
\frac{e^b}{N!}\max_{x\in[a,b]}\left|\prod_{j=1}^N(x-x_j)\right|
\le\frac{e^b h^N}{2^{N-1}N!}.
\]
The implementation converts the interpolant to a power basis, encloses that polynomial with Bernstein coefficients, then adds this remainder. The formula validates truncation over the continuum. The computed coefficients, transcendental values and bound endpoints remain unvalidated floating-point quantities, so the interface deliberately does not call the result certified. Degree is capped at eight in the lab to keep the conversion modest; high-degree basis conversion raises conditioning issues.
Interactive experiment: the same function and domain bounded by Taylor/interval evaluation, Taylor/Bernstein evaluation, and a Chebyshev interpolant with an analytic remainder.








Tool
What it supplies
What still needs attention




Taylor expansion
Local derivative-based polynomial and remainder
Domain radius, composition, truncation


Bernstein basis
A convex-hull enclosure of a polynomial
Coefficient computation, overestimation, subdivision


Chebyshev interpolation
An approximation distributed across a domain
Valid remainder, coefficient errors, polynomial range



These are compatible ingredients, not competing complete verification systems. The lab deliberately uses Bernstein bounds inside both approximation methods.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: 6. Replace a difficult graph with easier inequalities
text:
6. Replace a difficult graph with easier inequalities
Suppose carrying a polynomial becomes too expensive. We can instead carry constraints that every point on the graph must satisfy.
For \(z=xy\), with \(x\in[l_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[l_y,u_y]\), products of nonnegative endpoint distances give
\[
\begin{aligned}
z&\ge l_xy+l_yx-l_xl_y,\\
z&\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y,\\
z&\le u_xy+l_yx-u_xl_y,\\
z&\le l_xy+u_yx-l_xu_y.
\end{aligned}
\]
For instance, \((x-l_x)(y-l_y)\ge0\) gives the first inequality. The other three follow by using upper endpoint distances. These McCormick envelopes describe the convex hull of the scalar bilinear graph over a rectangle. Intersecting them with another relation, such as \(y=1-x\), remains a valid relaxation, but need not give the convex hull of the restricted graph.
For \(z=\operatorname{ReLU}(x)\) over \(l<0<u\), convexity gives the secant upper bound
\[
z\le\frac{u}{u-l}(x-l),\qquad
z\ge\alpha x\quad\text{for every }\alpha\in[0,1].
\]
The lower line works because \(\alpha x\le0\) for negative \(x\), and \(\alpha x\le x\) for positive \(x\). The full triangular relaxation keeps both \(z\ge0\) and \(z\ge x\); a single chosen lower line may be looser. Stable positive and negative neurons use their exact linear branches.
Interactive experiment: ReLU supporting lines and a McCormick slice. Change the objective or lower slope; inspect the accompanying IBP/CROWN-style network comparison.
DeepPoly (Singh et al.) associates neurons with affine lower and upper constraints, together with concrete intervals. Back-substitution exposes dependencies on earlier variables. CROWN (Zhang et al.) propagates bounds backwards for a selected output objective. In either case, coefficient signs matter: a positive coefficient uses an upper activation bound to bound an objective above, while a negative coefficient uses a lower bound.
Repeated substitution produces a linear expression \(a^Tx+b\). Its maximum over a centre-radius box is
\[
\max_{|x-c|\le r}(a^Tx+b)=a^Tc+b+|a|^Tr.
\]
The network experiment implements this backward substitution with IBP pre-activation intervals and fixed lower slopes. It is labelled CROWN-style, not a reproduction of a full verifier. A poor slope choice can make it looser than IBP. Optimizing per-neuron slopes, as in \(\alpha\)-CROWN, can improve an objective. This page does not implement that optimizer.
CROWN-IBP combines fast forward interval bounds with backward linear relaxation in robust training. It is an algorithmic combination, whereas a zonotope is a representation and subdivision is a refinement strategy. Keeping those categories separate helps explain which techniques can be used together.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: 7. When one pass is not enough
text:
7. When one pass is not enough
A coarse enclosure does not mean the specification is false. It may mean we have asked the bounding engine to cover too much at once.
Partition the domain into a complete cover,
\[
\mathcal X=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\mathcal X_k.
\]
If \(f(\mathcal X_k)\subseteq[L_k,U_k]\) on every leaf, then
\[
f(\mathcal X)\subseteq[\min_k L_k,\max_k U_k].
\]
This remains sound at every intermediate stage, provided no region is lost. Branch-and-bound adds decisions about which region to split and which regions can be dismissed using valid proof bounds. The experiment below implements the complete-cover subdivision core: split the widest local enclosure and retain every leaf. It does not claim an optimized pruning strategy.
Interactive experiment: refine x(1 − x) with natural intervals or a McCormick LP slice, and compare enclosure width with the number of bound evaluations.

What would a solver add?
A linear program (LP) can optimize an output subject to all affine-layer equations and activation relaxation inequalities at once. The bilinear experiment is a deliberately small LP that can be solved analytically: after \(y=1-x\) is substituted, envelope extrema occur at interval endpoints or crossings of two lines.
A semidefinite program (SDP) can retain quadratic relationships in a lifted matrix. For our recurring example, introduce \(X\) for \(x^2\):
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&x\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,
\quad 0\le x\le1,\quad X\le x.
\]
The constraint \(X\le x\) is the lifted form of \(x(1-x)\ge0\): multiply the two bound constraints \(x\ge0\) and \(1-x\ge0\), then replace \(x^2\) by \(X\). Positive semidefiniteness implies \(X\ge x^2\). Hence \(0\le x-X\le x-x^2\le1/4\). Both endpoints are achievable, so this small relaxation recovers the exact output range. In larger systems the lifted matrix need not equal \(xx^T\): dropping the rank-one constraint is a relaxation, not an exact reformulation.
For a crossing ReLU, a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) can encode its two branches using \(\delta\in\{0,1\}\):
\[
z\ge0,\quad z\ge x,\quad
z\le u\delta,\quad z\le x-l(1-\delta).
\]
With valid finite pre-activation bounds, \(\delta=0\) forces the inactive branch and \(\delta=1\) the active branch. Exhaustively resolving feasible branch assignments gives an exact real-arithmetic formulation of a finite piecewise-linear network. The one-dimensional network below enumerates its linear regions instead of invoking a general MILP solver. Tjeng, Xiao and Tedrake study scalable MILP verification.
SMT verification can ask whether a violating input exists under affine and activation constraints. Reluplex combines linear reasoning with ReLU case handling. An unsatisfiability proof excludes the encoded violation; a timeout is inconclusive. Numeric tolerances and proof checking still matter in implementations.
A star set, \(\{c+V\alpha:C\alpha\le d\}\), carries an affine map of a constrained predicate set. Splitting on the sign of a ReLU adds a predicate inequality to each branch. Exact splitting retains a union of stars; merging or relaxing those branches trades tightness for cost. These solver and set representations are explained here through small checkable examples; no general LP, SDP, MILP, SMT or star-set package runs in the browser.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: Moving up in complexity: a small network
text:
Moving up in complexity: a small network
We now compare the methods on one small network with fixed weights and a single uncertain input, holding everything else fixed. For the ReLU variant, enumerating its linear pieces gives the exact range, so every enclosure can be scored against it. Lipschitz and local Jacobian bounds provide sensitivity-based baselines.
Start from the defaults, then widen the input interval to see where each method loses precision.
Fixed-slope CROWN is looser than IBP here. Select one layer, ReLU, centre 0 and half-width 0.2. IBP gives approximately \([-0.09,0.25]\) (width \(0.34\)); fixed-slope CROWN gives \([-0.09,0.29]\) (width \(0.38\)), about 12% wider on the same problem.
Compare bounding methods on the same small network.
These results compare particular implementations and settings, not method families. Both endpoints matter as well as the width: one method can raise the lower bound while loosening the upper. A tighter enclosure may also cost more than the application can afford, so the experiment reports timings alongside widths.


When is an improvement guaranteed—and when is it only a hypothesis?

Nested enclosures guarantee no worsening. If two sound intervals \([L_1,U_1]\) and \([L_2,U_2]\) enclose the same nonempty output set, their intersection
\[
[\max(L_1,L_2),\min(U_1,U_2)]
\]
is sound and no wider than either. Keeping a baseline and intersecting new validated results makes the retained bound improve monotonically, even if candidate methods do not. Empty intersections indicate incompatible assumptions or an error; they cannot certify a nonempty reachable set. The browser’s floating-point fallback is described in the verification report.
Subdivision needs a monotone engine or retained parent bounds. For an inclusion-isotone enclosure \(B\), \(X'\subseteq X\) implies \(B(X')\subseteq B(X)\). Natural interval evaluation of a fixed supported expression has this property in real arithmetic. Splitting existing cells therefore cannot widen their combined enclosure. For a more general engine, intersect each child bound with its retained sound parent bound to enforce this property. Merely increasing the number of equal subdomains does not necessarily create a nested partition.
Added valid constraints help when the optimisation problem stays comparable. If feasible relaxations satisfy \(F_{\rm new}\subseteq F_{\rm old}\) and both contain the true graph, exact minimisation can only raise the lower bound and exact maximisation can only lower the upper bound. A finite-time solver may return weaker certified bounds if it has made less progress; keeping the previous valid result avoids losing that progress.
Higher degree, more generators, and new slopes need testing. Rebuilding a representation can change the remainder, range estimator, generator reduction or relaxation choices. The resulting enclosures need not be nested. A more accurate approximation is not automatically a tighter range enclosure, as the quadratic Taylor example shows. Numerical conditioning and validated rounding can add further width.
A research comparison changes one ingredient at a time. Fix the model, domain and objective; record lower and upper bounds, width and cost; use an analytic reference where available; and examine the cases where the proposed improvement loses. For a robustness claim, measure the relevant margin too. Stop when the required property is established or the remaining uncertainty is not worth the available computation.



Derivation: Lipschitz and local Jacobian bounds, fixed weights, and comparison metrics

Lipschitz bounds turn a domain-wide sensitivity bound into an output enclosure. For \(x\in[c-r,c+r]\) and \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|\) on this interval,
\[
f(x)\in[f(c)-Lr,f(c)+Lr].
\]
A product of layer norms and activation Lipschitz constants gives a simple bound. Using the selected domain can tighten it: the demo propagates absolute weights with per-neuron derivative magnitudes from IBP pre-activation intervals \([\ell,u]\). ReLU uses zero if \(u\le0\), otherwise at most one; square uses \(2\max(|\ell|,|u|)\). These local constants can be much smaller than global ones, though absolute values lose cancellations.
Jacobian-based local enclosures preserve derivative signs. On a convex domain,
\[
f(x)-f(c)=\int_0^1J_f(c+t(x-c))(x-c)\,dt.
\]
An interval enclosure of the Jacobian throughout the domain bounds the integral. For ReLU networks, use absolute continuity along paths and the almost-everywhere derivatives. Sign-aware propagation can improve an absolute sensitivity bound, but derivative intervals may still lose dependencies. A derivative evaluated only at the centre is insufficient.
Piecewise enumeration visits every reachable linear region of this scalar-input ReLU network; checking all region endpoints finds its extrema in real arithmetic. Polynomial / Bernstein propagation retains the full polynomial for square activations (degree two or four here) before bounding its range. The former pays for branches; the latter pays for polynomial terms and a potentially conservative range enclosure.
The fixed network has one or two width-three hidden layers:
\[
h_1=\sigma(W_1x+b_1),\qquad
h_2=\sigma(W_hh_1+b_h),\qquad
f=W_oh_j+b_o,
\]
where \(j=1\) or \(2\), with
\[
W_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\0.5\end{pmatrix},\quad
b_1=\begin{pmatrix}-0.2\\0.1\\0.3\end{pmatrix},\quad
W_h=\begin{pmatrix}0.7&-0.4&0.3\\-0.2&0.8&0.5\\0.4&0.2&-0.6\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
b_h=\begin{pmatrix}0.1\\-0.1\\0.05\end{pmatrix},\quad
W_o=\begin{pmatrix}1&-0.8&0.5\end{pmatrix},\quad b_o=0.05.
\]
No training or random weights are involved. See the network module.
The shared metrics are enclosure width \(W=U-L\), excess width \(E=W-(y_{\max}-y_{\min})\), and ratio \(\rho=W/(y_{\max}-y_{\min})\) only when the true width is positive. Excess and ratio require an exact reference range; they are not claimed for the square-network polynomial enclosure. Vector widths are componentwise. Browser timings indicate computational work in this implementation, not general complexity or a rigorous performance ranking.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: Does the diagnosis transfer to attention?
text:
Does the diagnosis transfer to attention?
The final test is whether the same reasoning holds for a different computation. Consider an attention head that forms queries, keys and values, then computes
\[
S=\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt d\,\tau},\qquad
A=\operatorname{softmax}(S),\qquad H=AV,
\]
where \(d\) is the key dimension and \(\tau>0\) is the temperature. Each stage discards dependence differently: the scores share input embeddings, the probabilities share one normalisation, and the values depend on the same inputs as the scores.
With two tokens, one relationship is particularly useful. The attention weights are \(p\) and \(1-p\), so
\[
h=pv_1+(1-p)v_2.
\]
By enforcing that the weights sum to one, we obtain an aggregation bound no wider than treating them independently, for the same probability and value intervals. The dependency-aware method also retains shared factors when bounding score differences. Softmax bounds
Can the predicted token change? After projecting the attention output to logits, the token is unchanged if
\[
\boxed{\text{winner's lower logit}>\text{every competitor's upper logit}.}
\]
The experiment changes one ingredient at a time:

At fixed radius and temperature, switch Interval to Dependencies + row sum. This isolates the effect of retaining dependence.
Enable subdivision. This spends more computation on the same problem.
Increase the radius. This makes the problem harder; it does not improve the method.

Bound a two-token attention head and inspect the greedy-token margin.
A narrower logit interval is not sufficient: the winner’s lower endpoint must clear every competitor’s upper endpoint. When it does not, the result is Inconclusive — either the bound remains too loose, or the winner genuinely changes within the input set, and bounds alone may not distinguish the two. When the inequality holds numerically, validated arithmetic is still required before it constitutes a certificate.
Scope. The head is small and fixed, with four artificial output tokens. Its perturbations are continuous shifts of embeddings, not paraphrases or whole generated responses.


Derivation: attention projections, score differences, softmax, aggregation, and logits

For two embeddings \(X\in\mathbb R^{2\times2}\), linear projections \(Q=XW_Q\), \(K=XW_K\), \(V=XW_V\) use the affine interval rule above. Each score is
\[
s_{ij}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^2Q_{ik}K_{jk}}{\sqrt2\,\tau},\qquad\tau>0.
\]
Natural interval products are cheap but forget shared embedding factors. Affine products and McCormick planes retain some of those relationships and can tighten the score bounds. The demo intersects these valid real-arithmetic enclosures; it does not solve a coupled global LP.
Softmax bounds follow from monotonicity. Rewrite a row probability as
\[
a_i=\frac1{1+\sum_{j\ne i}\exp(s_j-s_i)}.
\]
If \(s_j\in[\ell_j,u_j]\), increasing \(s_i\) increases \(a_i\) and increasing another score decreases it, so
\[
\frac1{1+\sum_{j\ne i}\exp(u_j-\ell_i)}\le a_i
\le\frac1{1+\sum_{j\ne i}\exp(\ell_j-u_i)}.
\]
These bounds are tight over an independent score box, which may include impossible score combinations. With two keys,
\[
a_1=\operatorname{sigmoid}(s_1-s_2),\qquad a_2=1-a_1.
\]
Bounding the difference before converting it to an interval retains cancellation in the shared query and keys. A sign-dependent sigmoid implementation avoids unnecessary exponential overflow. Increasing temperature scales down score differences, but does not guarantee a better final classification margin because the nominal output changes too.
Row-sum-aware aggregation exploits \(a_1+a_2=1\). Given \(p\in[p_-,p_+]\) and \(v_i\in[\ell_i,u_i]\), nonnegative weights make \(h=pv_1+(1-p)v_2\) increasing in each value. Its relaxed bounds are
\[
\underline h=\min_{p\in\{p_-,p_+\}}\{p\ell_1+(1-p)\ell_2\},\qquad
\overline h=\max_{p\in\{p_-,p_+\}}\{pu_1+(1-p)u_2\}.
\]
Only endpoint probabilities are needed because each expression is linear in \(p\). This is exact for the relaxed box in \((p,v_1,v_2)\) and avoids independent attention weights; remaining probability/value correlations can still make it loose.
Finally \(z=H_{2,:}W_O+b\) uses the affine interval rule. For nominal winner \(k\), define
\[
m=\underline z_k-\max_{j\ne k}\overline z_j.
\]
A validated \(m>0\) establishes an unchanged unique winner on the input set. Bounding each difference \(z_k-z_j\) directly can be tighter because shared terms may cancel; that extension is not implemented. A failed sufficient condition is inconclusive.
The artificial tokens sun, rain, wind and still have embeddings \((0.8,0.2)\), \((-0.5,0.7)\), \((0.1,-0.8)\) and \((-0.3,-0.2)\). Fixed projections are
\[
W_Q=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&-0.3\\0.2&0.7\end{pmatrix},\quad
W_K=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.4\\-0.5&0.9\end{pmatrix},\quad
W_V=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.2\\-0.3&0.8\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
W_O=\begin{pmatrix}1&-0.4&-0.7&0.2\\0.3&1&-0.2&-0.8\end{pmatrix},\quad
b=(0.12,-0.02,0.02,-0.08).
\]
One token’s coordinates vary independently by \(\pm\varepsilon\). The refinement option covers that two-dimensional box with \(4\times4=16\) subboxes, tightening local bounds at sixteen evaluations; such covers scale poorly with dimension. There are no residuals, normalisation, positional encodings, masks or feed-forward blocks. See the attention module.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
section: What a bound does and does not establish
text:
What a bound does and does not establish
A deterministic enclosure bounds where a fixed model’s output can go on a specified input set. A validated positive margin additionally establishes that the chosen class or token is unchanged. The enclosure bounds the model, not its error: neither statement says the prediction is correct.
Statistical coverage answers a different question: how often a prediction set contains the true outcome under stated sampling assumptions. Conformal prediction provides this, and we have applied it to spatio-temporal surrogates and, through the physics residual, without labelled data.


Different guarantees: randomised smoothing, conformal prediction, and discrete tokens

Randomised smoothing defines a new classifier by the most probable label of a base classifier under Gaussian noise. If \(p_A\) lower-bounds the winning label probability and \(p_B\) upper-bounds every competing label probability, then a standard Gaussian smoothing result gives an \(L_2\) robustness radius
\[
R=\frac{\sigma}{2}\left(\Phi^{-1}(p_A)-\Phi^{-1}(p_B)\right),\qquad p_A>p_B,
\]
where \(\sigma\) is the noise standard deviation and \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. Tighter probability bounds can improve the radius; Monte Carlo estimation introduces a stated failure probability and sampling cost. This certifies the smoothed classifier, not the base model’s deterministic output range. Randomised smoothing
Conformal prediction calibrates a prediction set against held-out scores. Under exchangeability of calibration and test data, a score rule fixed independently of the calibration labels, and the appropriate finite-sample quantile, it gives marginal coverage
\[
\mathbb P\{Y\in C(X)\}\ge1-\alpha.
\]
With \(n\) calibration scores, the split-conformal threshold is their \(\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\)-th order statistic, using \(+\infty\) if that index exceeds \(n\). Better predictive scores can produce smaller sets at the same coverage target. This improves statistical efficiency, not a deterministic enclosure on each input; marginal coverage is not conditional coverage at every \(X\). Conformal prediction
Discrete-token verification specifies allowed substitutions and then enumerates them or encloses their embedding images. A tighter representation of the allowed discrete set can exclude impossible continuous combinations and improve a robustness bound. The combinatorial cost can be large, and the chosen substitution set still requires a semantic justification. Neither a norm ball nor an unchanged token proves factual correctness or robustness to every paraphrase.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable
text:
Reproduce and extend
All experiments use local ES modules and SVG; there are no remote model calls or plotting dependencies. Each experiment has its own controls and reset button. The article remains readable with JavaScript disabled; equations use the site’s existing Quarto/MathJax setup.
The companion README documents the modules, fixed model and commands. The verification report separates real-arithmetic derivations, regression diagnostics and unimplemented formal validation. Run the JavaScript suite and the independent Python reference calculation before changing a mathematical kernel. The implementation deliberately uses reduced examples for constrained zonotopes, polynomial zonotopes and solver-based verification; it is not a general verification library.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable — verification report
text: Date: 26 October 2026. Scope: the new interactive article and its companion numerical modules.

title: Bounding the Unpredictable — verification report
text:
Guarantee audit
No browser calculation is machine-certified. All BoundResult objects have certified: false, including point domains, analytic-form reference ranges evaluated numerically, and positive transformer margins. Every experiment displays the floating-point limitation. A failed logit inequality is Inconclusive; a successful numerical inequality is Positive numerical margin — illustrative.
The paper-and-pencil formulas are inclusions under real arithmetic with a nonempty finite domain and the stated fixed model. Taylor and Chebyshev remainders bound mathematical approximation/truncation error. They do not bound floating-point coefficient, transcendental, summation or endpoint error. ReLU region enumeration is exact as a real-arithmetic procedure; its browser execution is still floating point.
A pair of enclosures that should intersect mathematically can be disjoint at a point domain due to cancellation. The implementation falls back to their hull (or the original natural product enclosure) instead of treating an inverted interval as meaningful. McCormick point slices similarly take the hull of computed edges if they invert. These robustness fallbacks do not establish directed-rounding soundness.
Samples are used only in regression diagnostics and drawings. They are never used to justify a certificate, choose an approximation-error bound, or prune a verification region.

Coverage includes polynomial residuals, network outputs, and attention Q/K/V, scores, probabilities, value aggregation and logits at corners and seeded interior points. title: Bounding the Unpredictable — verification report
text:
Scope and limitations

All nine experiments compute their displayed results from controls. No precomputed or fabricated robustness outcomes.
Constrained zonotopes use one analytically eliminable equality. Polynomial zonotopes use the exact quadratic image in the geometry experiment. Neither is a general set library.
The CROWN-style implementation uses fixed chosen lower slopes and IBP pre-activation bounds. It does not reproduce all of DeepPoly, CROWN-IBP training, or alpha-CROWN optimization.
LP is an analytic one-dimensional McCormick slice. General SDP, MILP, SMT and star-set solvers are not implemented. Refinement retains every leaf rather than performing branch pruning.
Chebyshev interpolation is supported for exp, where an explicit derivative remainder is available. Bernstein coefficient conversion can become ill-conditioned at high degree; UI degrees are capped at eight.
The network is scalar-input and width three. Square activation is a transparent polynomial benchmark, not a claim about commonly trained language models.
The attention head has no residual/normalization/position/masking stack. It verifies neither a pretrained model nor arbitrary natural-language substitutions. Componentwise logit bounds can lose more dependence than direct margins.
Input parameter ranges and refinement budgets are capped. Browser runtimes are illustrative and exclude rendering unless explicitly stated.
The existing site relies on externally loaded fonts and MathJax. The experiments themselves have no external numerical or rendering dependency.
